An Al Jazeera undercover team recorded middlemen offering to wash cash through the state gold refinery and export it as bullion. One of them was an ambassador-at-large. The government appointed a commission, and the practice continued. At one election, about 40 observers came from AFRIC, a group presenting itself as an independent African research body. Journalists later found it was organised by people linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin, founder of Russia's Wagner group. ZANU-PF is one of six parties that send officials to a party school in Tanzania funded by China's Communist Party. Rhodes Trust and BCCI are thought to have been active, but this is not documented. Zimbabwe is in the High band of the Global Organized Crime Index.
Zimbabwe.imp: A minister under US and UK sanctions now runs investment policy. The US says he misappropriated public funds, money residents would otherwise have received in services. If the state gold refinery is used to wash cash, Zimbabwe's gold exports carry criminal money. Voters were given election reports from observers who presented themselves as independent but were organised by people linked to Prigozhin.

Afghanistan.d: The Taliban have governed Afghanistan since 2021. The Haqqani network, a militant group within the Taliban, was given control of Kabul's security, and its leader Sirajuddin Haqqani became interior minister. In 2011 the top US military officer told the Senate the network acted as an arm of Pakistan's military intelligence service, the ISI. Pakistan denies ties. UN sanctions monitors reported in 2023 that at least three key Taliban government leaders are affiliated with al-Qaeda. In December 2025 they reported that al-Qaeda keeps a presence in several provinces. They also found that the Pakistani Taliban (TTP), with about 6,000 fighters, receives strong support from parts of the Taliban. The Taliban reject the reports. A Taliban figure listed by the US in 2012 for drug trafficking was later the movement's foreign-affairs chief and handled its relations with Iran. Before 2021, US and UN reports described provincial officials and police commanders taxing and protecting opium farming, and few cases reached a court. Ahmed Wali Karzai, the president's half-brother and head of the Kandahar provincial council, was described by US officials as part of the opium trade. He denied it, was never charged, and was killed in 2011. In 2012 the US listed two Kandahar money-exchange houses used by an opium network. Kabul Bank, which paid army and police salaries, lost about $935 million through loans to insiders. Its shareholders included brothers of the president and the first vice-president, and neither was charged. The bank's chairman and chief executive were jailed for five years.
Afghanistan.imp: Kabul's police and security are run by a group that a senior US commander tied to Pakistan's intelligence service. Armed groups that the UN lists as terrorist operate in several provinces with support from parts of the government. Before 2021, soldiers and police were paid through Kabul Bank, which its owners had emptied. Its rescue cost the state more than 5% of the economy's annual output.

Armenia.d: Samvel Karapetyan is a Russian-Armenian billionaire. His Tashir Group ran Electric Networks of Armenia, the country's only power distributor. He was detained on 18 June 2025 for public calls to seize power. He had backed the Armenian Church in its dispute with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. He was later also charged with money laundering. Parliament then passed amendments allowing the state to take over the grid company. His lawyers call the charges unfounded, and critics see a political case before the 2026 election. No trial result has been reported. This is the only documented case in Armenia, and it concerns an alleged plot rather than a proven one. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, has a documented presence. The Russkiy Mir Foundation, a Russian state foundation that promotes Russian language and culture abroad, is likely present, but no case is documented. Armenia is in the Low band for organised crime.
Armenia.imp: Every household in Armenia gets its electricity through one company. Its owner, a billionaire with a Russian base, is charged with calling for the government's overthrow, and parliament has given the state power to take the company. Residents face a dispute over who controls their power supply, alongside a criminal case that critics link to the coming election.

Azerbaijan.d: Azerbaijan hosted the UN climate summit, COP29, in November 2024. Its economy rests on oil and gas. The summit's president, Mukhtar Babayev, had been vice-president for ecology at SOCAR, the state oil company. The summit's chief executive, deputy energy minister Elnur Soltanov, was filmed in secret by the campaign group Global Witness. Its staff posed as investors, and he discussed possible oil and gas deals in the run-up to the talks. Critics said this broke the code of conduct for summit hosts. In June 2014 a company part-owned by SOCAR took over 11 high schools, 13 university-preparation centres and a private university linked to the Gülen movement. The Gülen movement is a Turkish religious network that Turkey's government pursues abroad. The takeover followed requests from Turkey's then prime minister, Erdoğan, for help against the movement. The company gave financial viability as its reason. Azerbaijan is also the home of the 'caviar diplomacy' network, which places Azerbaijani money inside European parliaments. Azerbaijan is in the High band for organised crime.
Azerbaijan.imp: Residents live in a country where officials from the state oil sector ran a UN summit on cutting fossil fuels. The people who decide on oil and gas deals also chaired the talks. Families with children in Gülen-linked schools saw those schools handed to a company part-owned by the state, after a foreign leader asked for it.

Bahrain.d: Nothing is documented yet of outside groups placing people or money inside Bahrain's government, so this is a best guess. Bahrain is in the Moderate band for organised crime. The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement, has a documented presence. Allies of Iran's Revolutionary Guards are likely present but undocumented. In the one documented case Bahrain acted abroad. It obtained an Interpol Red Notice, an international wanted alert, for Hakeem al-Araibi, a footballer living as a refugee in Australia. Thai police arrested him in 2018. Interpol withdrew the notice because its rules bar alerts sought by the country a refugee fled.
Bahrain.imp: With no documented case inside Bahrain, the cost to residents from outside groups is not known. The documented case shows the cost of Bahrain's own reach abroad. Bahrainis who flee and criticise the government can be arrested in a third country on an Interpol alert. Al-Araibi was held in Thailand for months until the case was dropped.

Bangladesh.d:
In Cox's Bazar, on the border with Myanmar, the trade in yaba (methamphetamine pills) has paid both local politicians and police. Abdur Rahman Bodi, the district's member of parliament, appeared on the government's own list of traffickers. In 2018 a court jailed him for three years for hiding his wealth; the trafficking claims never went to trial. In 2019, 102 dealers, several of them his relatives, surrendered at a staged ceremony.

In Teknaf, police running the anti-drug campaign killed hundreds of people in custody or in what they called crossfire. In 2022 a court sentenced a former station chief and several officers to death for killing a retired army major who had filmed them. The convictions were for murder, and the drug trade continued.

In February 2016, hackers inside Bangladesh Bank, the central bank, sent fraudulent payment orders worth $951 million from its account at the New York Federal Reserve. Most were blocked, but $101 million went out. US agencies tied the theft to a North Korean intelligence unit, and US prosecutors charged a North Korean programmer in 2018.

In January 2012 the army said it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, an Islamist group banned in Bangladesh since 2009. Bangladesh is in the High band for how easily officials can be bent.
Bangladesh.imp: People in Cox's Bazar and Teknaf live where the elected representative and the police have been tied to the drug trade they are meant to control. Residents there have been killed by the police in the name of fighting drugs, while the trade went on. The central bank theft took public money, and much of it has not been recovered.

Bhutan.d: Nothing is documented yet for Bhutan, so this is a best guess. No foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge has a documented presence in its government or firms. None is listed as likely to be present either. Bhutan is in the Low band of the Global Organized Crime Index, which rates crime and how well a state resists it. The estimate rests on that index alone. A documented case found later would replace it.
Bhutan.imp: With no documented case, there is no known cost to residents from outside groups placing people in Bhutan's offices or firms. The Low band means the index rates officials acting for outside interests as a smaller problem in Bhutan than in countries in the higher bands. Residents' main protection is that no such case has been found so far.

Brunei.d: Nothing is documented yet for Brunei, so this is a best guess. One outside presence is documented. Chinese police 'overseas service stations', offices linked to Chinese police forces that operate outside China, are listed as present in Brunei. No case describes what the station in Brunei does or who it contacts. No other foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge is listed. Brunei is in the Low band of the Global Organized Crime Index. The estimate rests on that index and on the single listed presence.
Brunei.imp: With no documented case, the cost to residents is not known. Chinese citizens living in Brunei are the people most likely to deal with a Chinese police office there. No case shows what such an office does for them or to them. Other residents have no documented exposure to outside groups placing people in Brunei's offices or firms. A documented case would change this.

Cambodia.d: Chen Zhi, born in China's Fujian province, became a Cambodian citizen in 2014 and built the Prince Group, one of Cambodia's largest conglomerates. He was an adviser to Hun Sen when Hun Sen was prime minister, and to the interior minister and the National Assembly president. In October 2025 US prosecutors charged him with running a fraud empire from scam compounds and seized about 127,271 bitcoin. The compounds hold trafficked workers in debt bondage to run investment fraud. The US and UK sanctioned people and firms linked to the group. In January 2026 Cambodia revoked his citizenship and sent him to China. In April 2026 the US sanctioned a sitting senator, Kok An, and his network over the same kind of compounds. Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of the people sanctioned. Hun To, a cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, is a major shareholder and director of Huione Pay, part of the Phnom Penh firm Huione Group. In 2025 the US Treasury found that Huione laundered over $4 billion, including money from North Korean hackers and scams. Cambodia's central bank had already revoked Huione Pay's licence. UNODC, the UN crime agency, describes casinos across the lower Mekong as a parallel banking system for drug, gambling and fraud money. The Unification Church gave Hun Sen a governance award in 2019 and a prize in 2022. In 2003 a military intelligence general was arrested with 35 kilograms of heroin and released within weeks.
Cambodia.imp: Workers trafficked into Cambodia's scam compounds are held in debt and forced to defraud people abroad. The owners have advised prime ministers and sat in the Senate, and Cambodian courts have charged none of them. A payment firm part-owned by the prime minister's cousin moved scam money, so residents' payments share a system with fraud proceeds. Casinos near the borders move money without bank records.

China.d: Chinese law requires any company with three or more Communist Party members to set up a party organisation. The party reported that 73.1% of private companies had one in 2018. Chinese partners of some foreign joint ventures asked the foreign side to write party groups into company articles. A leaked 2020 list of about 1.95 million party members showed members working in China for HSBC, Standard Chartered, Pfizer, AstraZeneca, Airbus, Boeing and Rolls-Royce. The list showed membership, not spying. ByteDance, which owns TikTok, has had a party committee since 2014, and a state fund took a board seat in 2021. ByteDance admitted in 2022 that staff used TikTok data to track journalists. JPMorgan hired about 100 relatives and friends of officials and state-company executives through its Hong Kong office from 2006 to 2013. It paid $264 million in 2016 to settle US bribery charges. ILSI, a group founded by a Coca-Cola executive and funded by food companies, had its China office inside the Chinese Center for Disease Control. A Harvard researcher reported in 2019 that it moved China's obesity policy toward exercise rather than diet. US courts have charged Chinese chemical companies with selling fentanyl ingredients to Mexican cartels. The companies are out of reach of US courts in practice. In Macau, the chairmen of the gambling junket firms Suncity and Tak Chun were jailed in 2023. Meng Hongwei, a vice-minister of public security, was Interpol's president until China detained him in 2018 and jailed him for bribery. In 1993 police minister Tao Siju said 'patriotic' triad members should be respected.
China.imp: People who work for private and foreign companies in China work alongside party organisations that the law requires. TikTok users' data was used by company staff to follow reporters. Advice on obesity reached the public through a body paid for by soft-drink and food makers. In Hong Kong, people attacked at Yuen Long station in 2019 waited 39 minutes for police to arrive.

Cyprus.d: Cyprus sold citizenship to foreign investors from 2007 to 2020. In October 2020 Al Jazeera broadcast an undercover film of House Speaker Demetris Syllouris and MP Christakis Giovanis. Both appeared willing to help a fictional Chinese investor with a money-laundering conviction obtain a Cypriot passport. Both resigned and the government closed the scheme. A state inquiry led by former judge Myron Nicolatos found that more than half of the passports had been granted unlawfully. Four men were sent to trial in 2022, and one was cleared in 2023. FBME Bank was registered in Tanzania and operated from Cyprus. In 2014 the US Treasury named it a primary money-laundering concern over accounts used by organised crime and sanctioned people. Cyprus took control of the bank and wound it down. Its owners challenged the US finding in arbitration for years. Cyprus is in the Moderate band for organised crime. The Trilateral Commission, a private forum of business and political leaders, has a documented presence. Grey Wolves, a Turkish ultranationalist group, is likely present but undocumented.
Cyprus.imp: For years Cypriot passports were sold to buyers who did not meet the rules, and the Speaker of parliament was filmed offering help. The state's own inquiry found most of those passports were issued unlawfully. Residents' banking system included an offshore bank that the US found served organised crime, and Cyprus had to take it over and close it.

Georgia.d: Bidzina Ivanishvili made his fortune in Russia in the 1990s. He founded Georgian Dream, the ruling party, and as its honorary chairman he nominates the prime minister. In December 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned him for 'undermining Georgian democracy and advancing the interests of the Russian Federation'. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia also sanctioned him. The European Parliament describes him as having 'personal and business links to the Kremlin'. He denies acting for Russia. The sanctions are decisions by those governments, and no court has tested the claims. The Gülen movement, a Turkish religious network, and the Grand Orient de France, a French Masonic body, have a documented presence. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, is also present. The Atlas Network, a group of free-market think tanks, is likely present but undocumented. Georgia is in the Moderate band for organised crime.
Georgia.imp: Georgians are governed by a party whose founder chooses the prime minister without holding office himself. The United States and three EU members say he serves Russia's interests, and they have sanctioned him. No Georgian court or inquiry has examined the claims, so residents have only the word of foreign governments and of Ivanishvili himself.

India.d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is a Hindu nationalist volunteer group founded in 1925. The governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) grew out of its political wing. Prime Minister Narendra Modi was a full-time RSS organiser before it sent him to the BJP in 1985. In 2020 the news site ThePrint counted 38 of 53 BJP ministers with RSS roots. Vice President C. P. Radhakrishnan has been with the RSS since age 16. Membership of the RSS is lawful. US prosecutors charged Gautam Adani, founder of the Adani Group, in 2024 with fraud over alleged bribes to Indian officials for solar power contracts. Adani denies the charges. France opened a corruption investigation in 2021 into India's purchase of 36 Rafale jets, after India's Supreme Court had found no irregularity. Italy acquitted the head of Finmeccanica over the AgustaWestland helicopter deal, which India cancelled. In 2024, 251 of 543 elected MPs declared pending criminal cases. Mukhtar Ansari won his Uttar Pradesh seat five times, much of that time from prison. Indian drug makers sold tapentadol, an opioid, to West African countries that had not approved it. Several Indian chemical firms are charged in the US with selling fentanyl ingredients for the Sinaloa cartel. Aviation minister Ram Mohan Naidu is in the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders class of 2025. US prosecutors say an Indian intelligence officer directed a 2023 plot to kill a Sikh activist in New York. In 1919 India's 'dyarchy' system came from a London Round Table study group, according to historian Carroll Quigley.
India.imp: Most of India's ministers come from one volunteer organisation that does not publish its members. Nearly half of the MPs elected in 2024 face pending criminal cases. US prosecutors have charged the founder of a conglomerate that runs ports, power and airports over bribes for solar power contracts. In Ghana, Nigeria and Côte d'Ivoire, opioids made in India and not approved there are sold in street markets.

Indonesia.d: Ma'ruf Amin, supreme leader of Nahdlatul Ulama, Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation, was vice-president from 2019 to 2024. He resigned the NU post before taking office. Pemuda Pancasila, a paramilitary group that took part in the 1965–66 killings, was part of the Golkar party from 1982 to 2001. Its members are known for extortion, parking-fee collection and protection work. Rolls-Royce and Airbus paid bribes to Emirsyah Satar, head of the state airline Garuda Indonesia. A Jakarta court jailed him for eight years in 2020. Monsanto paid a $50,000 bribe in 2002 to an environment ministry official assessing its genetically modified cotton. It settled with US authorities in 2005. Police inspector general Teddy Minahasa was jailed for life in 2023 for ordering seized methamphetamine to be sold on. His sentence was later reduced on appeal. The government banned Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia, which seeks a caliphate, in 2017 and warned that civil servants who were members would be dismissed. From 1966, economists trained at the University of California, Berkeley, on Ford Foundation grants ran Suharto's economy. Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency from 1967 to 1983, and Ali Wardhana was finance minister from 1968 to 1983. Their programme cut inflation and opened the country to foreign investors. John Perkins, an economist at the US firm Chas. T. Main, says he inflated forecasts so Indonesia would borrow. The claim is his own, and the New York Times found no evidence for parts of it.
Indonesia.imp: Garuda, the state airline, bought aircraft and engines from companies that bribed its chief. A police general sold drugs his officers had seized. Members of Pemuda Pancasila collect parking fees and protection money while tied to a governing party. For nearly two decades, economic policy was set by a team trained under a foreign foundation's programme.

Iran.d: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the country's ideological military force, owns large parts of the economy. Its engineering arm, Khatam al-Anbiya, controls more than 812 registered companies. It had received about 1,700 government contracts by 2012, in dams, tunnels, oil and gas fields and defence. The US, the EU and the UN Security Council list it as a Guards entity. In 2009 a consortium including Guards-linked foundations bought control of the Telecommunication Company of Iran. That company runs the fixed-line network and the largest mobile operator, which the state uses to monitor and filter communications. A Guards unit said in 2018 that it had sold its share. In 2025 a defence lawyer documented the conduct of two Tehran revolutionary court judges who hear drug cases and accused one of financial corruption. With no independent court, the claim cannot be tested. Iran is in the Severe band for organised crime. Before the 1979 revolution, General Nematollah Nassiri, head of the Shah's secret police SAVAK, signed the 1976 Safari Club pact. The other signers were the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco. Jafar Sharif-Emami, Grand Master of Iran's Masonic Grand Lodge, was the Shah's prime minister twice, the second time in 1978. In 1983 Ayatollah Khomeini attacked the Hojjatieh Society, a Shia religious society, and its affiliates were purged from government and education bodies.
Iran.imp: Iranians who use phones and the internet rely on a network that a Guards-linked group controlled for nearly a decade. Public works contracts go to companies owned by the Guards. People charged with drug offences, who can be hanged, are tried by courts that lawyers describe as dominated by the security services. Lawyers who challenge those judges report being targeted themselves.

Iraq.d: The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in 2014 to fight Islamic State. They are about 67 mostly Shia armed groups, almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. A 2016 law made them part of Iraq's armed forces, paid from the state budget. In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said publicly that it took orders from Iran's supreme leader. Kata'ib Hezbollah, listed by the US as a terrorist group since 2009, staffs three PMF brigades. The US linked it to a 2024 drone attack that killed three US soldiers. Falih al-Fayyadh chairs the PMF and was also national security adviser. The US sanctioned him in 2021 over the killing of protesters, and he remains chairman. A 2025 bill to tighten state control of the PMF was tabled under US pressure. In 2021–22 about $2.5 billion was taken from a tax commission account through fake refunds to five front companies. In 2024 a Baghdad court jailed a former MP and the former director of the prime minister's office. It sentenced businessman Nour Zuhair in absentia. A former governor's son who worked for the intelligence service was jailed for life for drug offences in 2018 and later pardoned. Captagon pills now cross a 600-kilometre border from Syria, and Iraq has become a production site.
Iraq.imp: Iraqis pay through the state budget for armed groups whose leaders say they follow Iran's supreme leader. One of those groups is listed as terrorist by the US and has drawn US strikes. About $2.5 billion of tax money was taken by people connected to the prime minister's office. Government employees, including teachers, now face mandatory drug tests as the captagon trade grows.

Israel.d: Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, is on trial for bribery, fraud and breach of trust in what is called Case 4000. Prosecutors say that while he was also communications minister, he gave regulatory decisions worth large sums to Shaul Elovitch, the controlling owner of Bezeq, Israel's largest telecoms company. In return, they say, Elovitch's news site Walla! gave Netanyahu favourable coverage. The trial began in May 2020. Netanyahu denies the charges and has asked President Herzog for a pardon. In 2025 police arrested two of his aides, Jonatan Urich and Eli Feldstein, on suspicion of taking money to promote Qatar's image in Israel. The money is said to have come through Third Circle, the firm of US lobbyist Jay Footlik. Qatar mediates in the Gaza war and hosts Hamas's political office. Netanyahu was questioned as a witness, not as a suspect, and calls the case a political witch hunt. Israeli courts have convicted police officers of passing investigation files to crime organisations. NSO Group, an Israeli company, sells Pegasus phone-hacking spyware to foreign governments under defence ministry export licences. Its clients used it against journalists and dissidents, and the US Commerce Department put NSO on a trade blacklist in 2021. The drug maker Teva agreed in 2022 to pay about $4.25 billion to settle US opioid claims, without admitting wrongdoing.
Israel.imp: People in Israel cannot be sure whether the news on a major site was shaped by a deal between its owner and the minister who regulated him. Advisers in the prime minister's office are under investigation for taking money linked to a foreign state that hosts Hamas's political office. Police officers have sold case files to crime families, which puts witnesses and people who report crimes at risk. Spyware made in Israel has been used abroad against reporters and activists.

Japan.d: In Japan, religious and nationalist groups have members and supporters among the ministers of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, elected in October 2025, has served in the Diet members' league of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby that wants to change the constitution. The Communist Party paper Akahata reported that 10 of her first 19 ministers were in that league. It counted 12 in the league of Shinto Seiji Renmei, the political arm of Japan's Shinto shrines, and five with ties to the Unification Church, a Korean-founded church. An LDP survey in 2022 found that 179 of its 379 Diet members had ties to the church. Some used church followers as campaign volunteers. Tokyo courts ordered the church's Japanese branch dissolved in 2025 for taking money from followers by unlawful pressure, and an appeal court upheld the order in March 2026. Komeito, the party of the Buddhist lay group Soka Gakkai, governed with the LDP for most of 1999 to 2025 and is now in opposition. Yakuza, Japan's organised crime groups, supplied workers to the state-funded Fukushima clean-up and took part of their pay. Mizuho Bank let car loans go to gang members for two years. Every prefecture now bars businesses from dealing with the gangs. A Diet commission found in 2012 that the nuclear regulator had been captured by TEPCO, the company that ran the Fukushima plant. A SoftBank employee was paid to give network manuals to a Russian trade official. The church's political ties go back to 1968, when former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi helped found its political arm.
Japan.imp: Voters in Japan elect lawmakers whose campaigns may have been staffed by followers of a church that a court found had pressured families into ruinous donations. Many cabinet ministers belong to lobbies that want to rewrite the constitution and change school teaching, and their membership is reported by the press, not disclosed by the government. Taxpayer money for the Fukushima clean-up partly went to gang recruiters. Residents near nuclear plants lived under a regulator that a parliamentary inquiry found was serving the operator.

Jordan.d: In Jordan, smugglers move captagon, an amphetamine pill, from Syria across the northern border, and some soldiers have helped them. Jordan's State Security Court has convicted serving and former soldiers of moving captagon and weapons across the border since 2022. Since Syrian production was disrupted in late 2024, smugglers have sent the pills by drone and then by large GPS-guided helium balloons that drop their loads once over the border. Jordan intercepted 128 balloon attempts between July 2025 and April 2026. The army has bombed production and storage sites inside Syria. In April 2025 the interior minister banned all activities of the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement, and said its assets would be seized. The ban followed arrests over an alleged weapons plot, which the group denied knowing about. The Brotherhood's political arm, the Islamic Action Front, won 31 of 138 seats in the 2024 election and is the largest party in parliament. In January 2026 the US Treasury listed the Jordanian branch of the Brotherhood as a terrorist group. Jordan's government says the group was dissolved years ago.
Jordan.imp: Families in northern Jordan live on a smuggling route where some of the soldiers paid to stop drugs have been convicted of moving them. Voters who chose the Islamic Action Front, the largest party in parliament, elected a party whose parent movement is now banned at home. The United States lists that movement as terrorist, and its members in Jordan face arrest and seizure of assets.

Kazakhstan.d: Kazakhstan has one documented case, and it concerns schools. After the July 2016 coup attempt in Turkey, Ankara asked Central Asian governments to close schools linked to the Gülen movement. This is a Turkish Islamic movement that Ankara blames for the coup. Kazakhstan declined to close them. In October 2016 the foundation that ran the schools, KATEV, renamed its 33 Turkish-Kazakh lyceums as 'Bilim' Innovative Lyceums. The schools had been set up with the Gülen movement. RFE/RL reported that no Kazakh government order lay behind the renaming. Opus Dei, a Catholic lay organisation, and the Order of Malta are also present. So are Hizb ut-Tahrir, a group that campaigns for an Islamic caliphate, and the Grey Wolves, a Turkish nationalist youth movement. No case ties any of them to Kazakh officials. Kazakhstan sits in the moderate band for organised crime.
Kazakhstan.imp: Parents and pupils at the 33 lyceums saw their schools renamed and their founders become the target of a foreign government's campaign. Kazakhstan refused Turkey's request to close the schools. Residents are otherwise affected mainly by the ordinary corruption and organised crime measured for the country, which this account does not document case by case.

Korea, DPR.d: North Korea's state runs hacking units, including the Lazarus Group, and a programme that places North Korean IT workers in remote jobs abroad. The Reconnaissance General Bureau, its foreign intelligence agency, is based in the country. The one documented case is the Pong Su. In 2003 this North Korean freighter delivered 125 kilograms of heroin to a beach in Victoria, Australia. Australian special forces boarded it. In 2006 a jury acquitted the captain and senior crew of importing the drug, because it was not persuaded they knew what the cargo was. The court never established that the North Korean state was behind the shipment. Australia later sank the ship as a bombing target. North Korea sits in the severe band for organised crime. The Unification Church, founded by a Korean, is listed as present in the North. No case documents what it does there, and no North Korean official appears in any court case.
Korea, DPR.imp: People in North Korea have no independent courts or press to examine what their state does abroad. The country sits in the severe band for organised crime, with officials acting for the state's own schemes. Money from state hacking and overseas IT work goes to the state. Residents cannot learn what the state did in the Pong Su case, because no North Korean court or paper examined it.

Korea, Rep..d: In South Korea, churches have paid politicians at the highest level. In August 2026 a Seoul court jailed Han Hak-ja, leader of the Unification Church, for two years. It found she arranged a diamond necklace and a Chanel bag for First Lady Kim Keon-hee in 2022 to seek favours. The court also found she paid 100 million won to Kweon Seong-dong, a senior lawmaker of the People Power Party (PPP). Kim was jailed in January 2026, and Kweon lost his seat after the Supreme Court upheld his two-year term. The church says it will appeal Han's sentence. In December 2025 the oceans minister, Chun Jae-soo of the Democratic Party, resigned after a church official said the church gave him cash and watches. Chun denies it. Prosecutors say Shincheonji, another church, registered at least 56,472 of its members as PPP members to influence its primaries; its founder Lee Man-hee was indicted in July 2026. Samsung's head, Lee Jae-yong, was convicted in 2017 of bribing President Park Geun-hye's circle, served his term and was pardoned. Prosecutors charge that a former Samsung executive used Chengdu government money to copy a Samsung chip plant in China. In 1978 a US congressional inquiry found the Unification Church made M-16 rifles for Seoul and acted for the South Korean government.
Korea, Rep..imp: South Korean voters have seen a first lady and a party floor leader jailed for taking church money in the run-up to the 2022 presidential election. Members of a church were signed up to a governing party in large numbers, which can change who wins its primaries. The country's largest business group bribed a president and its head was later pardoned. Prosecutors say Samsung's chip-plant designs were taken to China, which affects the jobs of Korean workers who built them.

Kuwait.d: In Kuwait, a party that grew from the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement, has sat in parliament and sometimes in the cabinet. After Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, the Kuwaiti Brotherhood broke with the international movement and founded the Islamic Constitutional Movement, known as Hadas. Hadas regularly won several seats in parliament in the 1990s and 2000s. Some of its members became cabinet ministers, which gave the movement a voice in setting policy. A coalition including Hadas left parliament after it boycotted the 2013 elections. Gulf state and private networks that fund Salafi religious missions are present in Kuwait. So is the Trilateral Commission, a private forum of business and political leaders. No case links these groups to payments or appointments in Kuwait's government. The Swedish telecoms firm Ericsson may also have operated there, but this is not documented. Kuwait sits in the moderate band for organised crime.
Kuwait.imp: Kuwaiti voters can elect a Brotherhood-derived party that works inside the constitution, unlike in Saudi Arabia, where the Brotherhood is listed as terrorist. Its members have held cabinet posts and so have helped set policy. When the party boycotts elections, its voters lose their representatives. Residents otherwise face the moderate level of corruption and organised crime measured for the country.

Kyrgyzstan.d: In Kyrgyzstan, a customs official and a crime boss have both been sanctioned by the United States while staying free at home. In December 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned Raiymbek Matraimov, a former deputy head of customs, for a smuggling scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country. Journalists from OCCRP and Kloop who reported on him were prosecuted or forced out. He settled a domestic corruption case by repaying money and served no prison term at the time. Kamchybek Kolbayev, a crime boss, was named a kingpin by the US in 2011. Kyrgyz courts repeatedly released him or gave him light sentences, and he was killed in a security operation in 2023. In 2021 Orhan Inandi, a Kyrgyz citizen who headed the Sapat schools set up by the Turkish Gülen movement, disappeared in Bishkek. President Erdogan later said he had been 'captured and taken to Turkey'. Kyrgyz military prosecutors opened a negligence case against border officers of the national security committee who let him be taken out.
Kyrgyzstan.imp: Customs revenue that should fund Kyrgyz schools and hospitals left the country through a smuggling scheme, and its organiser repaid part and avoided prison. Reporters who exposed it lost their jobs or left. Residents who live near crime groups saw courts release a known boss again and again. A Kyrgyz citizen was taken to Turkey past border guards who are now under investigation, so citizenship did not protect him.

Laos.d: In Bokeo province in northern Laos, a casino company run by a Chinese businessman administers a special economic zone. In 2007 the Lao government gave Kings Romans Group, owned by Zhao Wei, a 99-year lease to set up and run the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone. In 2018 the US Treasury sanctioned Zhao Wei's organisation for drug trafficking and money laundering through the zone. It said the Kings Romans casino stored and distributed drugs from Myanmar's United Wa State Army and laundered the proceeds. Zhao Wei denied this. The casino kept operating and expanding. The US State Department reports that criminal organisations control and administer the zone in part. No Lao official has been investigated, prosecuted or convicted over it. UNODC has linked the zone to cyber-fraud compounds and a river port built by a company tied to Zhao Wei. In February 2025 the Financial Action Task Force, which sets anti-money-laundering standards, put Laos on its list of countries under increased monitoring. Triads from Hong Kong and Macau are thought to be present but are not documented.
Laos.imp: Land in Bokeo was handed to a foreign casino company for 99 years, and residents there live under rules partly set by the zone's operators. Laos arrested more than 20,000 people for drug offences in five years while no official linked to the zone was charged. Banks in Laos face extra checks on international payments because of the monitoring listing, which can raise costs for ordinary businesses and people receiving money from abroad.

Lebanon.d: In Lebanon, Hezbollah, a Shia party with an armed wing aligned with Iran, holds seats in parliament and ministries in government. It has about 14 of 128 seats, and its picks run the health and labour ministries in the government formed in February 2025. With its ally Amal it controls six portfolios. In August 2025 the cabinet approved a goal that only the state hold weapons, and the army presented a plan to disarm Hezbollah. Hezbollah's leader rejected it. The US sanctioned two sitting Hezbollah MPs in 2019. Most large banks are owned by people tied to politicians. A 2016 study found 18 of the 20 major commercial banks had major shareholders linked to political elites. These banks lent heavily to the state and the central bank under Governor Riad Salameh, whose system collapsed in 2019 and froze depositors' savings. Salameh was detained in 2024 and charged with embezzling $42 million of public funds. Lebanese banks and exchange houses have moved cocaine money for networks in West Africa and the Americas. The Lebanese Canadian Bank's successor forfeited $102 million, and no banker was prosecuted. Captagon traffickers also operate. Nouh Zeaiter, sentenced to life and to death in absentia, got four months in February 2026 once in court. Saudi Arabia was reported to have held Prime Minister Saad Hariri in 2017 when he announced his resignation from Riyadh, which Saudi Arabia denied. In January 2026 the US listed al-Jamaa al-Islamiya, Lebanon's Muslim Brotherhood party, as a terrorist group.
Lebanon.imp: Lebanese depositors lost access to their savings when banks owned by politicians' associates collapsed after lending to the state. A party with its own army sits in government, so the state cannot decide alone on war and peace. Courts give known traffickers light sentences once they are in custody. Depositors who lost savings have seen the central bank governor charged, but no banker prosecuted for the cocaine money.

Malaysia.d: In Malaysia, a former prime minister has been convicted of taking money from a state fund that Goldman Sachs bankers helped raise. 1MDB was a Malaysian state investment fund. Goldman bankers Tim Leissner and Roger Ng arranged its bond sales with financier Jho Low. US authorities say money was diverted and used to bribe officials in Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates. Goldman paid Malaysia about $3.9 billion in a 2020 settlement, Leissner pleaded guilty and Ng was convicted in New York. In December 2025 Malaysia's High Court found Najib Razak, prime minister from 2009 to 2018, guilty on 25 counts tied to over $1 billion in his personal accounts. He was sentenced to 15 years and is appealing. Drug traffickers from the Golden Triangle pay police in Johor and the Klang valley. The anti-corruption commission has prosecuted narcotics officers for releasing suspects and reselling seized drugs. In May 2017 Malaysian police arrested three Turks at Turkey's request and deported them within days. Turkey accused them of links to the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic movement it blames for the 2016 coup attempt. Human Rights Watch condemned the deportations.
Malaysia.imp: Malaysians carry the cost of a state fund that lost billions while its money paid for a prime minister's accounts and foreign officials. People in Johor and the Klang valley live where some narcotics officers have sold seized drugs back onto the street. Foreign residents can be detained without trial and deported when another government cancels their papers.

Maldives.d: Nothing is documented yet for the Maldives, so this account is a best guess. The country sits in the moderate band of the Global Organized Crime Index. That band suggests some officials can be paid to serve outside business or criminal interests, and that the institutions meant to catch them have gaps. No case in the sources names a foreign state, company, church or crime group with people or money inside a Maldivian ministry, court or firm. Until such a case is found, any claim about who holds influence there is unproven.
Maldives.imp: If the index is right, residents may pay for weak courts and police through bribes, slow justice and contracts given to favoured firms. Without documented cases, people in the Maldives cannot point to who benefits. A stronger press and published court records would show whether outside interests are paying officials.

Mongolia.d: In Mongolia, the one documented case is an attempt by Turkey to remove a school director. On 27 July 2018 Veysel Akcay was seized in Ulaanbaatar. He was general manager of the Empathy Worldwide Educational Institution, which ran Turkish-Mongolian schools linked to the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic movement that Ankara blames for the 2016 coup attempt. Mongolian authorities grounded a plane at the airport, and he was released the same day. Turkish Minute and the Stockholm Center for Freedom reported that Turkey's intelligence service, MIT, carried out the abduction. Mongolian authorities said they had no specific knowledge of an abduction and were investigating. Chinese police 'overseas service stations', offices set up by Chinese police forces abroad, are also listed as present in Mongolia. No case documents what they do there. Mongolia sits in the moderate band for organised crime.
Mongolia.imp: People in Mongolia saw a foreign intelligence service reportedly try to take a resident from their capital, and their own authorities stop it at the airport. Teachers and pupils at the Turkish-Mongolian schools work under the risk that Turkey will pursue staff. Chinese police stations also operate in the country, and residents do not know what work they do.

Myanmar.d: In Myanmar's Shan State and along the Thai border in Karen State, armed groups allied with the military government run drug production and scam centres. Border militias formally placed under the army operate in the areas producing the most methamphetamine in the region. In Karen State, Colonel Saw Chit Thu led the Karen Border Guard Force, a militia under the army, and received a top state honour in 2022. He partnered with Chinese businessman She Zhijiang to build Shwe Kokko, a scam city using forced labour. The UK and US have sanctioned Saw Chit Thu. In the Kokang zone, Bai Suocheng, the zone's first leader and an MP for the army-backed USDP, ran scam and gambling centres with his family. Myanmar handed him to China, which in 2025 sentenced him, his son and three associates to death. The United Wa State Army built a business group, Hong Pang, with drug money. Buddhist nationalist monks of Ma Ba Tha wrote drafts that became four race and religion laws in 2015. These restrict conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men. The military government dropped sedition charges against the monk Wirathu and gave him a top honour. Myanmar is one of three countries on the Financial Action Task Force blacklist.
Myanmar.imp: People in Shan and Karen states live next to drug labs and scam compounds guarded by militias that the army treats as its own forces. Workers trafficked into those compounds are held and forced to defraud strangers. Muslim residents and Buddhist women face laws that limit whom they can marry and what religion they can choose. The blacklisting makes international payments hard for every business and family in the country.

Nepal.d: In Nepal, China's ambassador lobbied the ruling party's leaders during an internal revolt in 2020. That year, members of the Nepal Communist Party rose against Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli. In May and July, Chinese ambassador Hou Yanqi met Oli, President Bidya Bhandari and senior leaders Madhav Kumar Nepal and Jhala Nath Khanal. She reportedly urged them to keep the party united. Former ministers and diplomats called the meetings interference. In December 2020 China sent a delegation led by Guo Yezhou of the Chinese Communist Party's International Department, which handles ties with foreign parties. The Chinese embassy said it only wished to see the party united. The Unification Church and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), an Indian Hindu nationalist volunteer group, are also present in Nepal. The Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks, may also be active. No case documents the dealings of any of these groups with Nepali officials.
Nepal.imp: Nepali voters chose a ruling party whose internal disputes a foreign embassy tried to settle. Decisions about who leads the government were discussed with a foreign ambassador before the public heard of them. Nepal lies between China and India, and both countries' organisations are active there. Residents also live with the high level of organised crime and corruption measured for the country.

Oman.d: Nothing is documented yet for Oman, so this account is a best guess. The country sits in the moderate band of the Global Organized Crime Index. Two outside organisations may have had a presence in Oman. One is the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), a bank prosecuted in the United States in the early 1990s. The other is Le Cercle, a private political club also called Cercle Pinay. Neither presence is documented by a source. No case names any foreign state, company or group with people or money inside Omani offices or firms.
Oman.imp: If the index is right, Omani residents face a middle level of risk that officials favour outside business or criminal interests over their own. That can mean contracts awarded to favoured firms and crimes that go unpunished. Without documented cases, residents cannot tell who might benefit. Published court records and audits would show whether outside money reaches officials.

Pakistan.d: In Pakistan, the IMF, foreign governments and religious lineages have people inside the state. In May 2019, while Pakistan was negotiating an IMF bailout, Reza Baqir, an IMF staff member, was named governor of the central bank. He served until 2022. In December 2018 the Supreme Court ordered the government to ban the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic movement, and to hand its Pak-Turk schools to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation. Families who hold hereditary custody of Sufi shrines draw income and votes from devotees. Shah Mahmood Qureshi, custodian of a shrine in Multan, was foreign minister twice. In Karachi's Lyari district, gang leader Uzair Baloch led the Peoples' Aman Committee, which was aligned with the Pakistan Peoples Party that governs Sindh. A military court jailed him for espionage in 2020; the party disputes claims that its leaders protected him. The Khanani group, a Karachi exchange house, laundered money for drug groups and designated terrorist groups. Its head pleaded guilty in the United States in 2016. In 2012 a military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned group that tried to recruit officers for a coup. In 2019 Rana Sanaullah, a provincial law minister, was charged with heroin smuggling. He was acquitted in 2022 after the officer who filed the case disowned it.
Pakistan.imp: Pakistanis live under economic policy set during IMF talks, with an IMF staff member running the central bank in those years. Voters in shrine areas such as Multan may back shrine families out of religious duty rather than policy. Karachi residents in Lyari lived under a gang that worked with the provincial ruling party. Drug charges have been used against a political opponent, so a case in court may not mean a crime took place.

Philippines.d: In the Philippines, churches deliver votes and their leaders have taken government posts. Iglesia ni Cristo, a Philippine church of about 2.6 million members, tells members how to vote. In 2022 it endorsed Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Sara Duterte and 12 Senate candidates. President Rodrigo Duterte named its head, Eduardo Manalo, a special envoy in 2018. Apollo Quiboloy, founder of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ church and Duterte's spiritual adviser, was arrested in 2024 on child-abuse and trafficking charges. Chinese-run online gambling firms (POGOs) were licensed from 2016, and Senate hearings tied many to fraud, trafficking and torture. Alice Guo, mayor of Bamban in Tarlac, was found to be a Chinese citizen and jailed for life for trafficking in 2025. Former presidential spokesman Harry Roque faces trafficking warrants over a POGO hub in Pampanga, which he denies. Congress banned POGOs in 2025. State Grid Corporation of China owns 40% of the national power grid operator and names its chairman. Pharmally, a firm with ₱625,000 in capital, won ₱8.68 billion in pandemic contracts. Its chairman told senators that Michael Yang, a former Duterte adviser, backed its suppliers; Yang denies formal ties. Police in the drug war killed thousands, and Duterte was surrendered to the International Criminal Court in 2025. A senator who investigated the killings was jailed for almost seven years on drug charges that were later dismissed.
Philippines.imp: Filipino voters in Iglesia ni Cristo are told whom to vote for, which can decide close Senate races. Towns like Bamban had a mayor serving a gambling compound where trafficked workers were held. Electricity for the whole country moves through a grid partly owned by a Chinese state company. Pandemic money went to a firm with little capital. Families of people killed in the drug war have waited years for a court to hear their cases.

Qatar.d: Qatar's documented cases concern another Gulf state acting against it. In late May 2017 hackers took over Qatar's state news agency and government social media and posted false quotes from Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani praising Hamas and Iran. On 5 June Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Egypt and Bahrain cut ties with Qatar. The Washington Post, citing US intelligence officials, reported that senior UAE officials discussed the hacks the day before they happened. The officials could not say whether the UAE did the hacking or paid for it, and the UAE called the report false. Project Raven, a UAE surveillance unit operated by the firm DarkMatter, hired former US intelligence staff. Reuters reported in 2019 that it targeted the Emir of Qatar's phone. Three former US operatives later paid $1.68 million under agreements with the US Justice Department. Qatar is also suspected of paying for influence abroad. In Israel, aides to the prime minister are under investigation for taking money to promote Qatar's image.
Qatar.imp: Qatar's residents went through a blockade in 2017 that cut land and air routes after a hack planted false statements in their emir's name. Phones of senior officials were targeted by a neighbouring state's hackers, so private communications in Qatar may not be safe from foreign surveillance. Residents also live in a state accused of paying aides of a foreign prime minister.

Saudi Arabia.d: In Saudi Arabia, the crown prince's government has taken assets from business owners, and the state has paid for religious missions and intelligence networks abroad. From November 2017 a new anti-corruption committee under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman held princes and business leaders at the Ritz-Carlton in Riyadh. Among them were the chairmen of Saudi Binladin Group and the broadcaster MBC. The government says settlements with 87 people recovered about $107 billion in property, companies and cash. Some detainees said they were beaten. Saudi Arabia receives captagon pills smuggled from Syria and Lebanon through Jordan and Iraq. It executed 330 people in 2024, many of them foreign couriers convicted of drug offences. No Saudi official appears in any court case over the trade. In 2014 the government listed the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist group. In 1974 the US and Saudi governments set up a joint economic commission. A Saudi account in the US Treasury paid for its US technical advisers, and it sent US goods and services to Saudi Arabia. In 1976 intelligence chief Kamal Adham signed the Safari Club pact with France, Egypt, Morocco and Iran. Adham later fronted BCCI's secret purchase of a Washington bank and paid a $105 million fine.
Saudi Arabia.imp: Saudi business owners know the state can detain them and take their companies without a public trial. Foreign workers who carry drugs face execution while those who organise the trade are not named in court. Members or supporters of the Muslim Brotherhood risk prosecution as terrorists. Saudi residents have little way to check how state money spent abroad on religion or intelligence is used.

Singapore.d: Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry expelled Huang Jing, a US-citizen professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, in 2017. It called him an agent of influence who worked with a foreign country's intelligence agents to shape Singapore's foreign policy. It did not name the country, and Huang denied the charge. In 2024 the ministry used its foreign-interference law to designate Philip Chan Man Ping, a Hong Kong-born businessman. He led the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in Singapore and was patron of two government-linked grassroots groups. He had also attended a Chinese Communist Party united front body as an overseas delegate. He must now disclose his donations and foreign links. Asiaciti Trust, a Singapore offshore services firm named in the Pandora Papers, was fined by the Monetary Authority of Singapore for anti-money-laundering failures. It has not been charged over drug money. Courts convicted 32 men in 2025 alone for holding or moving drug proceeds, and the sentences include prison and caning. Glenn Defense Marine Asia, a Singapore ship-supply firm run by Leonard Francis, bribed US Navy officers with cash, travel and gifts for years. A civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore stopped an early inquiry into it. Francis was sentenced in the United States in 2024.
Singapore.imp: Residents who lead community or business groups with ties to China can be named by the government and made to report their donations and foreign contacts. An academic can lose residence with no public trial. People caught moving small sums of drug money go to prison, while offshore firms that hide who owns companies have so far faced fines. Navy bribery by a local supplier was exposed and punished by US courts, not Singapore's.

Sri Lanka.d: Bodu Bala Sena (BBS, 'Buddhist Power Force') is a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist monks' group accused of stirring violence against Muslims. In 2013 Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, the president's brother, opened its training centre in Galle District as chief guest. After he became president, Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed the group's leader, the monk Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, to chair a presidential task force on a single legal code. The justice minister said he had not been consulted. The Bar Association said the task force would take over the work of Parliament and the Justice Ministry. Gnanasara had been jailed for contempt of court in the case of a disappeared journalist, Prageeth Eknaligoda, and President Maithripala Sirisena pardoned him. In September 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that pardon invalid, and the Court of Appeal ordered him to serve the rest of the sentence. Ranil Wickremesinghe, president from 2022 to 2024, is listed as a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market discussion society. No body has found that the society directed his decisions. The arrest in Dubai of a Sri Lankan drug trafficker, Madush, produced photographs of him at a party with police officers and politicians. He was killed in police custody before an inquiry finished.
Sri Lanka.imp: Muslim residents saw a monk accused of stirring hatred against them put in charge of proposals to rewrite the country's laws. A presidential pardon freed him from a court sentence, which showed supporters that a court ruling could be set aside by the president. The 2026 Supreme Court ruling restores a limit on that pardon power. Police officers photographed with a trafficker faced an inquiry that never ended, so residents cannot know which officers worked with him.

Syria.d: Until December 2024, the Assad family and the army's Fourth Armoured Division made and exported captagon, an amphetamine pill. In 2023 the United States, Britain and the European Union sanctioned Maher al-Assad, the president's brother and the division's commander, and three of the president's cousins. The US Treasury said one cousin's plant in Latakia province made 84 million pills in a year. A sitting member of parliament, Amer Khiti, was sanctioned over companies that produced and moved the pills. The EU also listed private security companies used as covers for pro-government militias in the drug trade. These are government sanctions, not court verdicts. In August 2026 a Damascus court sentenced Bashar al-Assad and his brother to death in absentia for murder, torture and crimes against humanity. The charges did not cover drugs. Both men live in Russia, which refuses to extradite them, and Human Rights Watch questioned whether the trial was fair. Since the government fell, reporting says drug production has moved to Sweida province, where local armed groups run laboratories and smuggling routes. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force advised and commanded alongside Assad's army from 2012, with Hezbollah fighters in combat. Iran withdrew its commanders when Assad fell. Lafarge, the French cement maker, paid the Islamic State and al-Nusra Front to keep a plant in northern Syria running in 2013–14. It pleaded guilty in the United States, and a Paris court convicted the company and several former executives in 2026.
Syria.imp: For over a decade, the state's army and the president's family earned money from making and smuggling drugs, so police and courts did not act against the trade. Iranian officers commanded garrisons on Syrian soil alongside the Syrian army. A foreign company paid armed groups for road access while they controlled the area. Since 2024 the drug trade has moved to armed groups in Sweida, and the former leaders cannot be tried in person because Russia keeps them.

Taiwan.d: In 2025 the Taipei District Court jailed Chou Ke-chi, chairman of the small Gong He Party, and two association officials. It found they used money from Fujian to fund the party's 2022 local campaigns. A Chiayi court jailed Lin Hsueh-feng, a former KMT council candidate, for taking village chiefs on trips to Zhejiang paid for by a Chinese city's Taiwan affairs office. Four former members of the governing DPP were convicted of spying for Chinese military intelligence. They included an aide to Foreign Minister Joseph Wu and a Presidential Office consultant, and they passed on William Lai's travel schedules. In 2026 the High Court jailed Hu Peng-nien, a retired cabinet official, for trying to recruit military personnel for China's united front system. Former legislator Chang Hsien-yao is charged, not convicted, with taking Chinese instructions in the 2024 presidential race. Most of these rulings can still be appealed. The Interior Ministry has asked to dissolve the Chinese Unification Promotion Party, founded by former Bamboo Union gang leader Chang An-lo. It cited espionage, election interference and 98 organised-crime cases linked to members. Former TSMC engineers passed secrets on its 2-nanometre chip process to a Tokyo Electron employee to help that company win orders. A court jailed them in 2026 and fined Tokyo Electron's Taiwan unit. Israel's Mossad used a front company to license the brand of Taiwan's Gold Apollo for the pagers that exploded across Lebanon in 2024. Taiwan is also the headquarters of the World League for Freedom and Democracy, formerly the World Anti-Communist League, a Cold War alliance.
Taiwan.imp: Village chiefs, small parties and local candidates have taken Chinese money or trips, so voters cannot be sure whose interests a local candidate serves. Aides with access to the president's travel plans passed them to Chinese intelligence, which affects the safety of elected leaders. A party with gang ties is being taken to the Constitutional Court. Theft of chip secrets threatens the jobs and income that depend on TSMC. A Taiwanese brand was used without its public knowledge in a deadly attack abroad.

Tajikistan.d: In 2012 a military court in Khatlon province jailed five Border Guard officers for up to 21 years. The longest term went to the former chief of the Vakhsh checkpoint on the Afghan border, where investigators had found hashish in his office. A senior Khatlon police official was arrested the same day carrying heroin. In 2000 Tajikistan's ambassador to Kazakhstan was arrested in Almaty with heroin in his car. At a later trial, prosecutors argued that a deputy interior minister had been murdered for refusing to pay for a drug consignment. That claim is an allegation and was not proven against named officials. Estimates in 2014 put drug money at up to 30 percent of the country's economy. Most seizures are of small dealers, and no conviction in these cases goes above border-guard and provincial police rank. The Gülen movement is a Turkish religious movement that Turkey's government calls the terrorist group 'FETÖ'. It ran seven schools in Tajikistan until President Emomali Rahmon closed them by decree in 2015 and handed them to the state. The Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a documented presence. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Tajikistan in its Severe band.
Tajikistan.imp: Border guards and police paid to let drugs pass make the Afghan border a smuggling route rather than a check. If drug money makes up a large share of the economy, many residents depend on it for work and prices, and officials who refuse to cooperate face danger. Families whose children attended the Turkish-run schools saw them taken over by the state with little notice.

Thailand.d: Senator Upakit Pachariyangkun was indicted in 2023 on drug trafficking and money-laundering charges. The charges are linked to a Myanmar businessman arrested in Bangkok, whom the US has sanctioned for supporting Myanmar's military government. The senator's son-in-law was among those arrested, and the narcotics board seized property worth over 400 million baht from his homes. The case has not reached a verdict. In the same year, the deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over alleged protection of an online gambling network. The case split the police leadership in public. In 2017 the administrator of AlphaBay, an online drug market closed by US and European police, was arrested in Bangkok. He died in custody a week later, so the evidence against him was never tested. Paetongtarn Shinawatra was named to the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders class of 2025 while she was prime minister. The programme is a five-year series of meetings and courses run by the Davos forum, and selection is not wrongdoing. The Constitutional Court removed her from office in August 2025. Two Cold War-era groups, the World Anti-Communist League and the Unification Church, a South Korean religious movement, also have a documented presence.
Thailand.imp: A senator charged over drug money sat in the upper house that votes on laws. When a deputy police chief is accused of protecting gambling operators, residents cannot be sure which police complaints will be followed up. The death of the AlphaBay administrator in custody means people in Thailand never heard the evidence against him. Property seized from the senator's homes shows how much drug money can end up in Thai real estate.

Timor-Leste.d: In 2004 Australia's foreign spy service, the Australian Secret Intelligence Service (ASIS), planted listening devices in Timor-Leste's government offices in Dili. It wanted to learn Timor-Leste's position in talks over oil and gas fields in the Timor Sea. The treaty that followed, CMATS, limited Timor-Leste's sea claims. A former ASIS officer, known as Witness K, disclosed the operation. In 2013 Australia raided his home and the office of Timor-Leste's lawyer, Bernard Collaery. Timor-Leste took Australia to the International Court of Justice and the Permanent Court of Arbitration. In 2014 the International Court of Justice ordered Australia not to interfere with Timor-Leste's legal communications. A new boundary treaty in 2018 replaced CMATS and gives Timor-Leste 80 percent of the revenue. Witness K pleaded guilty to a secrecy offence in 2021. The case against Collaery was dropped in 2022. Aginter Press, a Cold War anticommunist intelligence front that posed as a news agency, and the Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also have a documented presence. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Timor-Leste in its Moderate band.
Timor-Leste.imp: Timor-Leste depends on Timor Sea oil and gas for public money. For about a decade, the CMATS treaty gave its people a smaller share of that revenue after Australia spied on their negotiators. The 2018 treaty raised the share of public money that comes to Timor-Leste. The man who revealed the spying was prosecuted in Australia, so officials elsewhere who see wrongdoing against Timor-Leste have reason to stay silent.

Turkiye.d: Turkey's government designates the Gülen movement, a religious movement, as the terrorist group 'FETÖ' and blames it for the July 2016 coup attempt. Since then about 150,000 people have been dismissed from public jobs by emergency decree, including judges, officers and police. The state trustee fund took over 784 companies it called Gülen-linked, including Bank Asya, and later returned more than 600. Courts have given life sentences to air force officers as leaders of the coup. The Diyanet, Turkey's state religious directorate, had its imams abroad report on Gülen followers in other countries. Interpol refused 773 Turkish arrest-notice requests against Gülen suspects as political. In the earlier Ergenekon and Sledgehammer coup-plot trials, courts convicted hundreds of officers, MPs and journalists. Higher courts later overturned those verdicts, finding no evidence Ergenekon existed and forged evidence in Sledgehammer. The government now blames those prosecutions on Gülen-linked police and prosecutors. The Grey Wolves are the youth wing of the nationalist MHP party, now the AKP's partner in government. Their leader Alparslan Türkeş was deputy prime minister in the 1970s. In 1996 a car crash at Susurluk killed a deputy Istanbul police chief and a wanted Grey Wolves gunman. The gunman carried a passport and gun licence signed by the interior minister. A parliamentary inquiry found that state bodies had used the Grey Wolves. A sentencing law passed by the AKP and MHP freed crime boss Alaattin Çakıcı, whose amnesty the MHP leader had demanded. During the Cold War the army housed Counter-Guerrilla, a NATO stay-behind unit paid by the United States until the mid-1970s.
Turkiye.imp: About 150,000 public employees lost their jobs, and many owners lost businesses, on the government's word that they had Gülen links, often without a conviction. Judges who fear removal are less likely to rule against the government. Earlier, officers and journalists spent years in prison on evidence later found forged. A crime boss allied with a governing party was freed by a law that party helped pass. Turks abroad may be reported on by state-paid imams.

Turkmenistan.d: In 2011 Turkmenistan closed or nationalised most of the schools that the Gülen movement had opened there in the 1990s. The Gülen movement is a Turkish religious movement that ran schools in several former Soviet states. Turkey's government calls it the terrorist group 'FETÖ'. In late 2016 Turkmen security services detained more than 100 people, most with some Gülen affiliation. Eighteen men were then convicted in closed trials and given 12 to 25 years for inciting hatred and belonging to a criminal organisation. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Norwegian Helsinki Committee reported the sentences in a joint statement in 2017. Because the trials were closed, the evidence has not been made public. The Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a documented presence. No case has been documented of a foreign state or company placing people inside Turkmenistan's government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Turkmenistan in its Severe band. It gives a high score for officials acting for outside interests and a low score for courts, police and watchdogs.
Turkmenistan.imp: Teachers, parents and former pupils linked to the Turkish schools can be detained and tried in secret. Families of the men sentenced have no public account of the evidence against them. With weak courts and watchdogs, residents have little way to challenge officials who act for outside interests, or to find out whether they do.

United Arab Emirates.d: The UAE gave Interpol's foundation about $54 million, reported to equal the regular dues of all other member countries combined. Its interior ministry inspector general, Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, was then Interpol's president from 2021 to 2025. French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry into complaints that he was responsible for the torture of detainees in UAE custody. He denies this. Sultan Al Jaber, chief executive of the state oil company ADNOC, presided over the COP28 climate talks. Leaked briefing papers prepared for his meetings with foreign governments included talking points on ADNOC business deals. The US has sanctioned Dubai exchange houses and trading firms that moved money for a Helmand heroin network and other sanctioned networks. Dubai free-zone companies can keep their real owners hidden from the public. A Bosnian trafficker used them to employ men prosecutors call his gang's operatives. The UAE was on the FATF grey list for weak anti-money-laundering controls from 2022 to 2024. A US task force concluded that the gold refiner Kaloti bought metal from suspected drug launderers, but the Treasury dropped the case and the company denies it. North Korean state hackers stole about US$1.5 billion from Bybit, a Dubai crypto exchange, through a software supplier. Earlier, Abu Dhabi's ruler, ruling family and government owned most of BCCI, a bank closed for fraud. A US Senate report found Abu Dhabi kept the fraud from the bank's auditors for months. At home, the government jailed members of Islah, a local Islamist group, and lists the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist.
United Arab Emirates.imp: Money from drugs, sanctions-busting and theft can be placed in Dubai companies with owners hidden from the public, which raises property prices and puts honest firms at a disadvantage. Residents and visitors who allege torture in UAE custody face an interior ministry whose senior officer led Interpol. Emiratis who join Islamist groups risk long prison terms. The state oil company's chief presided over UN climate talks while his team prepared oil and gas talking points for meetings.

Uzbekistan.d: Three foreign telecom companies paid Gulnara Karimova, daughter of then-President Islam Karimov, to enter Uzbekistan's mobile market. The payments went to companies she controlled, in return for licences and radio frequencies. VimpelCom, Telia and MTS each settled US foreign-bribery cases between 2016 and 2019. Telia, the Swedish-Finnish group, agreed to pay about $965 million to US, Dutch and Swedish authorities in 2017. Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at 869.3 million dollars. OCCRP, a journalists' network, reported that she took over $1 billion from Scandinavian and Russian telecom firms. Karimova was convicted in Uzbekistan in 2017 and 2020 and remains in prison. Switzerland dropped its own trial against her in 2026. Chinese police 'overseas service stations', offices that Chinese police run abroad, have a documented presence in Uzbekistan. Turkey's Gülen movement, the Grey Wolves, a Turkish nationalist group, and Hizb ut-Tahrir, an Islamist party, are likely present but not documented. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Uzbekistan in its High band. It gives a high score for officials acting for outside interests.
Uzbekistan.imp: Uzbek mobile users paid for a market whose licences were sold through the president's daughter instead of through open bidding. The settlement money went mainly to US, Dutch and Swedish authorities, not to Uzbekistan. Weak courts and watchdogs leave residents with few ways to challenge officials who act for outside interests.

Vietnam.d: In Hanoi, two former officers of a district drug investigation team were indicted in 2024 for shielding a Laos–Vietnam drug network. That network moved 137 kilograms of drugs. In Viet Tri, a senior police officer was sentenced to life in 2025. He had paid for a large purchase of drug tablets that he planned to use in a staged arrest. Vietnam executes traffickers caught with such amounts. Viet Tan is a pro-democracy party founded by Vietnamese exiles and based in the United States. In 2016 Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security declared it a terrorist organisation. The ministry said it trained people to enter Vietnam and plotted sabotage. Human rights groups and foreign governments dispute this, and the US government has said there is no evidence it is a terrorist group. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of membership. Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay members, has a documented presence. Novartis, a drug company, and Ericsson, a telecom firm, are likely present but not documented. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Vietnam in its High band.
Vietnam.imp: Residents cannot count on drug police to enforce the law when some officers protect traffickers or stage arrests for credit. People face the death penalty for drug amounts that officers themselves have handled. Vietnamese who contact or support Viet Tan can be jailed as terrorism suspects, even though other governments do not treat the party as terrorist.

Yemen.d: The United Arab Emirates helped form the Southern Transitional Council (STC) in 2017, a group seeking a separate state in southern Yemen. In 2022 the STC joined Yemen's eight-member Presidential Leadership Council, the country's top governing body. Its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, became a vice-president. In December 2025 the STC launched an offensive, and Saudi-backed forces launched a counter-offensive. Al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council. A delegation in Riyadh announced the STC's dissolution, which its UAE-based spokesman rejected. Hezbollah, Lebanon's armed movement, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force with its allied militias also have a documented presence. So do the Muslim Brotherhood and DarkMatter, a UAE cyber-surveillance company. Several foreign states' influence networks are documented as well. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Yemen in its Severe band. It gives Yemen a score of 1.9 out of 10 for courts, police and watchdogs.
Yemen.imp: Residents of the south were governed in part by a council whose leader depended on the UAE and now lives there. Fighting between UAE-backed and Saudi-backed forces in late 2025 put civilians in the middle. With courts and police too weak to act, residents have no body to complain to when armed groups backed from outside take land or money.

Australia.d:
Huang Xiangmo, a property developer, chaired a council described as a peak body for groups linked to the United Front Work Department, the Chinese Communist Party office that organises influence abroad. With associates he gave about AU$2 million to Labor and over AU$1 million to the Liberal Party. In 2015 his cash reached NSW Labor's Sydney office disguised as donations from restaurant staff, the state anti-corruption commission found. A company linked to him paid the legal bills of Labor senator Sam Dastyari, who resigned in 2018. The government cancelled Huang's residency on security-service advice in 2019. In Melbourne, community leader Di Sanh Duong was convicted in 2023 of preparing foreign interference aimed at a federal minister. Officers of India's intelligence service, RAW, cultivated politicians and a state police service, and two were expelled in 2020, media reported in 2024.

In Sydney and Melbourne, courts have convicted Border Force and state police officers who helped drug importers. Criminal money moved through Commonwealth Bank deposit machines and through Crown Resorts and The Star casinos, which all paid penalties or settled. In Victoria, bikie gang members held roles in the CFMEU construction union on state-funded building sites, and the federal government put that division into administration in 2024. A PwC partner hired by the Treasury to advise on tax-avoidance laws shared its confidential plans with other PwC partners. In Darwin, Landbridge, owned by a businessman with close ties to the Chinese Communist Party, holds a 99-year lease on the port.

Sydney's Nugan Hand Bank employed retired senior US military and intelligence officers before it collapsed in 1980. A Round Table group, part of a British imperial policy network, met in Australia from 1910.
