Australia.imp: Residents pay when officials act for others. Border and police officers paid by importers let more drugs into Sydney and Melbourne. Banks and casinos that failed to report criminal cash made it easier to launder drug profits. Donations from a foreign-linked donor bought access to state and federal politicians. Treasury's tax-avoidance plans were shared inside PwC, the same firm that advised the companies those laws targeted. Workers on Victorian public building sites dealt with bikie gang members in union posts.

Fiji.d: China's Ministry of Public Security placed its own officers inside the Fiji Police Force. A police cooperation agreement signed with China in 2011, while Fiji was under military rule, allowed this. From 2013 China attached two officers at a time to the Fijian force. In 2021 it posted a police liaison officer to its embassy. In 2017 Chinese police, working with Fijian officials, arrested 77 Chinese nationals in Fiji and flew them to China. In March 2024 Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua said Fiji had asked China to withdraw the embedded officers. He also said Fiji would keep the agreement and review it every six months. Fijian police officers continue to train in China. China gets police contacts in Fiji and help in returning people it wants back. Other groups with documented presence include Shincheonji, a South Korean church, and organisations acting for the Chinese state that are not named as United Front bodies. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, an Indian Hindu nationalist organisation, is likely present but no case is documented. Fiji's drug intelligence chief has also raised concern that drug traffickers have recruited people in law enforcement.
Fiji.imp: People in Fiji were policed for years by a force that included officers answering to a foreign ministry. Chinese nationals living in Fiji were arrested and sent to China with help from local officials. Officers trained in China may bring its policing methods back. The agreement stays in force, so Fiji can invite Chinese officers back without a new vote.

Kiribati.d: Uniformed Chinese police officers work inside the Kiribati Police Service. Kiribati moved its diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019. In 2022 it asked China for help with policing. In 2024 acting police commissioner Eeri Aritiera confirmed to Reuters that up to a dozen Chinese officers work alongside local police. They serve six-month rotations. They do community policing, teach martial arts and give IT support for a crime database. China gets officers on daily duty in a Pacific state that recently switched its recognition away from Taiwan. It also gets a role in building the database Kiribati uses to record crime. The arrangement came to light because the Kiribati police confirmed it to journalists. Organisations acting for the Chinese state, not named as United Front bodies, have a documented presence. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, is also present. No case of officials being paid by an outside group is documented here.
Kiribati.imp: People in Kiribati may be stopped or questioned by officers who answer to a foreign government. Information in the police crime database is handled with Chinese technical help, so residents cannot know who sees it. The local force relies on outside training and staff, which makes it harder to say no to further requests.

Marshall Islands.d: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, China-born businesspeople who had bought Marshallese passports, paid bribes to Marshall Islands officials, including members of parliament. The payments ran from about 2016 to 2020 and totalled tens of thousands of dollars. They wanted a law creating the 'Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region', a semi-autonomous zone. Both pleaded guilty in a New York court. Zhou was sentenced in February 2023 and Yan received 42 months in prison in May 2023. In December 2023 the US State Department barred former president Kessai Note and MP Mike Halferty from entering the United States for taking those bribes. That is a decision of the US government, not a court verdict. Note denies taking money. The scheme came to light through the US prosecution and reporting by OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists. No one has been charged in the Marshall Islands. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a documented presence.
Marshall Islands.imp: Lawmakers took money to pass a law that would have set up a special zone on Rongelap for the people paying them. The people of Rongelap would have been governed under a law written to suit those buyers. Passports sold to outsiders gave them legal standing to deal with officials. The case was prosecuted abroad, so local accountability depends on foreign courts.

Micronesia.d: In March 2023 David Panuelo, then president of the Federated States of Micronesia, wrote a 13-page letter accusing China of 'political warfare'. He said China used bribery and threats against Micronesian officials. He wrote that the aim was to keep Micronesia aligned with Beijing, or neutral, if war broke out over Taiwan. He said he had considered switching recognition from China to Taiwan. China rejected the claims. These are allegations from a sitting president, and no court or inquiry has tested them. No official has been named as taking money. The letter was made public by Reuters and CNN shortly before Panuelo left office. China would gain a friendly or neutral government in the event of a war over Taiwan. Organisations acting for the Chinese state, not named as United Front bodies, have a documented presence. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, is also present.
Micronesia.imp: If the president's account is true, some officials took money or gave way to threats when making foreign policy. Micronesians would then have leaders whose choices on war and security were bought from outside. Since nothing has been investigated, residents cannot tell which officials, if any, were involved. They also cannot judge whether later decisions on Taiwan and security were made freely.

Nauru.d:
Australian companies have paid money to Nauru's politicians while seeking business there. Getax Australia, a phosphate trader based on the Gold Coast, is charged by Australian federal prosecutors with conspiring to bribe Nauruan politicians between 2007 and 2012. It wanted phosphate deals. The case has been delayed many times and has not reached a verdict. In a related case, Sydney businessman Mozammil Bhojani pleaded guilty to paying over 120,000 dollars to a Nauruan MP and a minister and was jailed in 2018.

Australia pays contractors to run its asylum detention centre on Nauru. In 2023 the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age reported that subcontracts worth millions went to firms tied to Nauru's leaders. They found banking records showing suspect payments to justice minister David Adeang. They also reported about 2.6 million dollars going to a company of Lionel Aingimea, who later became president. The reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes, and Adeang denies wrongdoing. They reported that Australia's Home Affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations since 2010.
Nauru.imp: Phosphate is one of Nauru's few sources of income, and bribes for phosphate deals cut what the public receives. Money from detention contracts went to firms tied to leaders rather than to public budgets. Ministers who benefit from Australian contracts have reason to keep the detention centre running whatever residents think.

New Zealand.d:
Jian Yang, a National Party MP from 2011 to 2020, had been a Communist Party member and taught at Chinese army institutions that trained intelligence linguists. Media reported in 2021 that he retired after intelligence agencies raised concerns about his relationship with the Chinese government. The same reports said Labour MP Raymond Huo also left Parliament for that reason, with agreement from both party leaders.

SkyCity casino agreed a NZ$4.16 million penalty in 2024 for failing to monitor high-value play. New Zealand has the highest methamphetamine prices in the world, and casino floors are one place drug cash enters the economy.

Several senior politicians have belonged to international policy networks. Ruth Richardson, finance minister from 1990 to 1993, is a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market economists' club. Former prime minister Jacinda Ardern took part in the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme. David Seymour, deputy prime minister since 2025, earlier worked for a Canadian think tank that partners with the Atlas Network, which funds free-market think tanks. Membership of these lawful groups is not wrongdoing, and no inquiry has found that they directed government decisions.

A Round Table group, part of a British imperial policy network, met in New Zealand from 1910.
New Zealand.imp: Voters elected MPs whose links to a foreign government were known to intelligence agencies but not to the public until later. Weak checks at casinos let drug profits, earned from some of the world's highest prices, pass into legal money. Policy on tax, regulation and spending has been set by people trained in a small number of private networks, which residents did not choose.

Palau.d: Wan Kuok-koi, known as 'Broken Tooth', is a former head of Macau's 14K triad, a criminal gang. The US Treasury sanctioned him in 2020 and said he sits on a Chinese Communist Party United Front body. OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, reported in 2022 that he visited Palau in 2018 as a 'guest of the government'. A former postmaster general and a former governor of Airai state became directors of his Palau Hongmen association. The association was registered in early 2019. It planned a casino zone on the island of Angaur. In April 2019 President Tommy Remengesau opposed the casino. The association then applied to dissolve. OCCRP did not establish that the Chinese state directed the effort. No one in Palau has been charged. Hong Kong and Macau triads such as 14K, Sun Yee On and Wo Shing Wo are likely present but undocumented.
Palau.imp: Former senior officials lent their names to a gang leader's company, which gave it local standing. A casino zone on Angaur would have brought large amounts of gambling money, run by a sanctioned gang leader, to a small island community. The plan stopped because the president refused, not because of any law that blocked it.

Papua New Guinea.d:
In 2020 a Cessna carrying 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed on a makeshift runway outside Port Moresby. The police commissioner then said there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary and promised to remove them. The Australian-based organisers were convicted in Victoria, and the pilot was jailed for 18 years in PNG. The officers alleged to have helped the night flights were not charged.

In 2014 the government of Prime Minister Peter O'Neill borrowed about 1.2 billion US dollars through the bank UBS to buy shares in Oil Search. It did this against cabinet advice and before parliament approved it. Treasurer Don Polye objected and lost his job. A Commission of Inquiry found the loan unlawful in 2021 and recommended a 10-year ban on UBS. O'Neill was later charged with giving false evidence to the inquiry.

Paladin was paid by Australia to run its asylum centre on Manus Island from 2017 to 2019. Its former director told Australian newspapers in 2023 that money went to a Singapore account of a businessman close to senior PNG officials. He said an invoice marked 'Visas' was a bribe. Paladin's former chief executive denies any improper payment.
Papua New Guinea.imp: The state lost about 432 million dollars on the UBS loan, while the bank earned fees and interest. That is money that did not go to schools, clinics or roads. Police officers who helped drug flights still serve, so residents cannot rely on the force. Contracts paid by Australia for the Manus centre may have enriched officials rather than local people.

Samoa.d: No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Samoa is documented yet, so this is a best guess. The one organisation with a documented presence is Shincheonji Church of Jesus, a South Korean religious movement. Its presence is lawful and is not evidence of wrongdoing. The Global Organized Crime Index places Samoa in its Low band. It scores Samoa's courts, police and watchdogs somewhat higher than its exposure to officials acting for outside interests. Pressures seen in nearby states, such as foreign police agreements or bribes for business deals, may also occur here without having come to light.
Samoa.imp: Without documented cases, residents in Samoa have no specific harm from outside interference to point to. The risk is that pressures seen in neighbouring states, such as foreign police deals or bribes for contracts, go unnoticed here. Samoa's courts, police and watchdogs are the bodies that would need to bring such cases to light, and they score in the middle range.

Solomon Islands.d:
In September 2019 Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare ended 36 years of diplomatic ties with Taiwan and recognised China. MPs told The Guardian and the Solomon Star that both Beijing and Taipei had offered them money to sway the vote. Anger over the switch fed riots in Honiara in November 2021.

China then funded a discretionary fund run by the prime minister's office, as Taiwan had done before. In 2022 the prime minister's secretary told a parliamentary committee that China provided about US$2.49 million spent in 2021. He said 39 of the 50 MPs received payments, in two rounds in late 2021. Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote that December. Opposition leader Matthew Wale said the money kept him in power, which Sogavare's office denied.

China sent police advisers in February 2022 and signed a security agreement that lets the government ask for Chinese police and military personnel. In 2025 Chinese police began a local trial of the 'Fengqiao' model, a Chinese system of neighbourhood surveillance policing. It was suspended after local objections. In May 2026 Wale became prime minister and promised to review the security agreement.
Solomon Islands.imp: MPs were paid from a foreign-funded account in the weeks before a vote on whether the prime minister kept his job. Voters cannot tell whether their MP's choices were made for them or for the payer. Residents may be policed with Chinese help and Chinese methods under an agreement that parliament did not debate in public.

Tonga.d: Before 1997 Tonga sold passports to Hong Kong residents and put the money into the Tonga Trust Fund. In 1999 King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV named American financial adviser Jesse Bogdonoff his court jester. Bogdonoff moved the fund's money into a firm dealing in viatical settlements, which buy life insurance policies from people who are ill. That firm went bankrupt in 2002. Tonga lost about 33 million dollars, around 40% of a year's state revenue. The government sued him. In 2004 he settled the case without admitting fraud. This case is historical, but the passport-sale industry still has a documented presence in Tonga. Selling citizenship gives foreign buyers legal status and travel rights, and gives the state cash that can be spent with little oversight. No current case of outside groups paying officials is documented. The Global Organized Crime Index places Tonga in its Moderate band and gives it 6.0 of 10 for officials acting for outside interests.
Tonga.imp: Tongans lost money the state had raised for public use, equal to a large share of a year's budget. The decision to hand it over was made by the king and one foreign adviser, with no public vote. Passport sales continue to bring in outsiders whose loyalty to Tonga is untested.

Tuvalu.d: No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Tuvalu is documented yet, so this is a best guess. No foreign organisation has a documented presence here. The Global Organized Crime Index places Tuvalu in its Minimal band, with a low score for officials acting for outside interests. Its courts, police and watchdogs score in the middle range. Neighbouring Pacific states have seen foreign police agreements and bribes for business deals, and none of these is documented in Tuvalu.
Tuvalu.imp: With no documented cases, residents face no known harm from outside interference now. The risk is that foreign police agreements or bribes for contracts, seen in neighbouring states, arrive here unnoticed. Courts, police and watchdogs score only in the middle range, so such cases may take time to come to light.

Vanuatu.d: China has sent police advisers to Vanuatu since 2023. On 19 September 2025 Vanuatu's internal affairs minister, Andrew Solomon Napuat, met China's Minister of Public Security, Wang Xiaohong, in Beijing. China donated police equipment worth about NZ$720,000, including motorcycles and drones. The two sides said they were discussing a wider policing partnership. This was reported by Pacific Media Network. No wider agreement has been reported as signed, and its terms are not known. The police advisers sent since 2023 work with Vanuatu's force, though their exact role is not described. China gets working contacts with Vanuatu's police and a say in how they are trained and equipped. The same pattern has led to Chinese officers serving inside the police forces of Fiji, Kiribati and Solomon Islands. Organisations acting for the Chinese state, not named as United Front bodies, have a documented presence. No case of officials taking money from an outside group is documented.
Vanuatu.imp: Police in Vanuatu now use drones and vehicles supplied by China, with training from Chinese advisers. Residents may be watched with Chinese-donated drones whose data handling they cannot check. Decisions on the partnership are being made between ministers, without public debate. If a wider pact is signed, Chinese officers could take part in local policing, as they have in neighbouring states.

Albania.d: A 2015 'decriminalisation' law bars people with serious convictions, at home or abroad, from elected office in Albania. Seven MPs had resigned or been removed under it by 2020, most for hiding convictions. Elvis Roshi, mayor of Kavaja, lost office over an Italian drug-trafficking record. Since 2017 an EU-monitored vetting of every judge and prosecutor has removed or forced out about half of those assessed, mostly over unexplained wealth. Saimir Tahiri, interior minister until 2017, was convicted of abuse of office in 2019. Italian police had arrested his cousin in a probe into an Albanian-Italian cannabis group, and wiretaps mentioned Tahiri. The drug-trafficking charges against him were dropped. In 2026 Albania's special prosecutor seized assets and traced cocaine money into coastal land and high-rise towers in Tirana. Its order refers to meetings with senior state officials it does not name. One plot involved is land for a resort promoted by US investors. Albania hosts members of the Iranian opposition group MEK at a camp near Tirana. In 2022 a cyberattack shut down many government online services. Albania and the US found that Iran organised it, and Albania cut diplomatic ties. Iran called the finding baseless.
Albania.imp: Residents have seen MPs, mayors and judges removed because of criminal records or unexplained wealth. The courts they use are being rebuilt by that vetting. Cocaine money spent on Tirana flats and coastal land raises prices for local buyers. An interior minister whose cousin moved cannabis was punished only for abuse of office. Iran's cyberattack cut residents off from government online services for a time.

Andorra.d: Under Andorra's 1993 constitution, the president of France is one of the country's two heads of state, called co-princes. The other is the Bishop of Urgell, and Emmanuel Macron has held the French role since 2017. Acting alone, the French co-prince appoints a member of the Constitutional Tribunal and of the Superior Council of Justice. He must also agree to treaty texts. Jointly with Andorra's head of government, he appoints that head of government, calls elections and signs laws into force. A personal representative acts for him in Andorra. In 2015 the US Treasury named Banca Privada d'Andorra a primary money-laundering concern. It said senior managers moved money for Russian and Chinese crime groups and Venezuelan launderers. Andorra took over the bank the next day and wound it up within a week. The US withdrew its finding the following year, and Spanish courts dismissed related laundering cases. In July 2025 an Andorran court sentenced 18 executives, the former chief executive to seven years. They are appealing. Shareholders say the bank was closed on an administrative finding never tested in court.
Andorra.imp: A foreign head of state, elected only by French voters, takes part in choosing Andorra's head of government and judges. Andorrans have no vote on who holds that role. Clients of the closed bank had to prove their money was legitimate before they could recover it. Some lost access to savings for years on the strength of a US finding that was later withdrawn.

Austria.d: In May 2026 a Vienna court convicted Egisto Ott, a former officer of Austria's old domestic intelligence agency, of spying for Russia. He worked through Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive. Ott searched police databases for people Moscow wanted to find and handed over work phones from the interior minister's office. He plans to appeal. The Freedom Party (FPÖ) signed a cooperation agreement with Vladimir Putin's United Russia party in 2016. Its ministers sat in government from 2017 to 2019, and the agreement lapsed in 2021. Karin Kneissl, foreign minister for the FPÖ, later joined the board of Rosneft, Russia's state oil company, and now lives in Russia. ATIB, the Austrian branch of Turkey's state religious directorate, employs imams in Austrian mosques. In 2018 the government reviewed the residence permits of about 40 of them under a law banning foreign funding of religious bodies. Austria banned the salute of the Grey Wolves, a Turkish nationalist group, in 2019. Raiffeisen Bank International faces European Central Bank and US scrutiny over its Russian exposure; no penalty for drug money has been imposed. Former chancellor Sebastian Kurz is a World Economic Forum Young Global Leaders alumnus, which is a selection and not wrongdoing. In the Cold War, union leader Franz Olah ran a secret anticommunist force and later became interior minister. The US hid more than 80 weapons caches in Austria without telling its government. Police raids on suspected Muslim Brotherhood networks in 2020 were later ruled unlawful.
Austria.imp: A former intelligence officer gave Russia the addresses of people it wanted to find, including a journalist, which put people living in Austria at risk. A governing party had a formal pact with Russia's ruling party while its ministers ran ministries. Muslim residents have seen mosques closed and imams' permits reviewed over Turkish state funding. Residents raided as suspected Muslim Brotherhood members were later told by a court the searches were unlawful.

Belarus.d: After Belarus's disputed 2020 election, Vladimir Putin promised President Alexander Lukashenko a 1.5 billion dollar loan. In February 2022 Russian forces launched part of their invasion of Ukraine from Belarusian territory. A referendum that same month removed Belarus's constitutional ban on nuclear weapons and allowed permanent Russian bases. Russia supplied nuclear-capable Iskander-M missiles in 2023, and Putin said nuclear warheads were delivered. He has said Russia keeps control of them. Both governments state these arrangements in joint statements by their presidents. Belarus's army now works alongside Russian forces on its own soil, and the decision to use the warheads is Moscow's. The Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, has a documented presence. Russkiy Mir, a Russian state foundation that promotes Russian language and culture abroad, is likely present but not documented. Interpol and Hizb ut-Tahrir are in the same category. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Belarus in its Severe band. It gives Belarus a high score for officials acting for outside interests and a low score for courts, police and watchdogs.
Belarus.imp: Belarusians live in a country used as a launch point for the invasion of Ukraine and now host Russian nuclear weapons they cannot control. That makes their territory a possible military target. The Russian loan after the disputed 2020 election went to the same government that now hosts Russian forces. Weak courts and watchdogs leave residents no independent body to question these agreements.

Belgium.d: In Antwerp, cocaine gangs pay port workers, customs staff and police to move containers and pass on information. Antwerp courts have convicted people from all three groups, and three serving police officers were arrested in January 2024. The port seized 116 tonnes of cocaine in 2023. In Brussels, Belgian prosecutors charged Eva Kaili, then a Parliament vice-president, and others with taking cash to favour Qatar and Morocco. She denies it, and the case continues. In 2025 prosecutors charged people over gifts and football tickets allegedly given to MEPs to favour Huawei, the Chinese telecoms company. Foreign governments have also placed their own people in Brussels mosques. In 2020 Belgian intelligence found Moroccan intelligence members and a Diyanet employee, Turkey's state religious office, in the new body set up to run the Great Mosque. The justice minister refused it state recognition. A former Flemish senator, Frank Creyelman, was reported in 2023 to have taken money from a Chinese state security officer for three years. A gap in Belgian law blocked his prosecution. According to the Snowden documents, Britain's GCHQ broke into Belgacom, the majority state-owned telecom company, from 2010 to 2013. Saudi Arabia ran the Great Mosque from 1967 until Belgium ended the lease in 2018. During the Cold War, a secret NATO stay-behind network was run by military intelligence and State Security until the government disbanded it in 1990.
Belgium.imp: Cocaine gangs can pay Antwerp port staff and police to pull containers and pass on information. In 2022 the justice minister was put under police protection after a kidnap plot. EU decisions taken in Brussels affect everyone in the union, and prosecutors in two bribery cases allege that foreign states and a company paid MEPs. Muslim residents have seen their main mosque run by Saudi, Moroccan and Turkish state appointees in turn.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d: Under the 1995 Dayton peace deal, a High Representative who answers to a council of foreign governments can impose laws and dismiss Bosnian officials. By 2004 the office had dismissed 139 officials. The current High Representative, Germany's Christian Schmidt, took office in 2021. Russia, China and some Bosnian politicians say his appointment is illegitimate. In Republika Srpska, the Serb-run half of the country, Russia backs the former entity president Milorad Dodik. Its police signed a 2016 cooperation agreement with Russia's interior ministry on intelligence and counter-terrorism. Dodik met Vladimir Putin at least five times from 2022 and received a Russian state order in 2023. The United States sanctioned him and his family firms, then lifted the sanctions in October 2025. A Bosnian court banned him from politics for six years in 2025 for defying the international envoy. In Sarajevo, 23 people were arrested in April 2024 for trafficking and laundering money for a cocaine boss already sentenced in the Netherlands. Europol said corrupt officials who helped the group were among those detained. The envoy's powers date from 1997, two years after the peace deal ended the war.
Bosnia and Herzegovina.imp: Bosnians vote for officials whom a foreign-appointed envoy can remove, and for laws the envoy can override. In Republika Srpska, the police work with Russia's interior ministry under a written agreement. Officials arrested in Sarajevo in 2024 were helping a cocaine group launder money. Residents who deal with officials cannot always tell whether those officials also work for a criminal group.

Bulgaria.d: Bulgarian smuggling groups pay customs and border officials on the Balkan route into the European Union. In June 2021 the United States sanctioned Bulgarian officials and business figures, several in customs and border posts, over smuggling protection. It was the largest action of its kind the US has taken against one country. Bulgarian prosecutors have charged few of them. In Sofia, a man known as 'the Notary', Martin Bozhanov, is alleged to have collected compromising files on judges and prosecutors and used them to pressure them. Bulgarian National Radio reported that he threatened prosecutors as well as judges. Former Prosecutor General Ivan Geshev was questioned in the case. The claims are under investigation and have not been tested in court. Prosecutors charged Nikolay Malinov, a former MP who leads Bulgaria's largest pro-Russia group, in 2019 with collecting state secrets for RISS, a Russian state think tank. While on bail he travelled to Moscow, where Putin gave him a Russian state award. A Sofia court acquitted him of all charges in May 2026.
Bulgaria.imp: When customs and border officers take money from smugglers, goods cross the border without proper checks. If the claims about 'the Notary' are true, judges and prosecutors under pressure may decide cases for whoever holds the files on them. The few prosecutions after the 2021 US sanctions leave residents with little proof that paid officials are removed.

Croatia.d: MOL, Hungary's state-influenced oil company, wanted management control of INA, Croatia's national oil company. Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive, Zsolt Hernádi, to give it that control. The first verdict, in 2012, was quashed in 2015. Sanader was convicted again in 2020, and the Supreme Court confirmed the conviction in 2021. Hungary has not handed Hernádi to Croatia, and MOL denies paying the bribe. Croatia is in the Moderate band for organised crime. Several outside groups are present in the country without any documented case of them placing people in office. They include Opus Dei, a Catholic lay movement, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, and the Trilateral Commission, a private forum of politicians and executives. Patria, a Finnish defence maker, also appears among the organisations with a presence.
Croatia.imp: Croatians own a national oil company whose management a foreign firm won by paying the head of government, according to the courts. The man the courts found paid the bribe lives in Hungary, which has not handed him over. The conviction of the prime minister did not change who manages INA. Croatia's courts could punish the official who took the money but not the executive who paid it.

Czech Republic.d: Prime Minister Andrej Babiš owns Agrofert, a farming, food and chemicals group that receives EU farm subsidies. A European Commission audit published in 2021 found he still controlled Agrofert while in office and was in a conflict of interest. He became prime minister again in December 2025. In February 2026 he moved the shares to a new trust and said the conflict was resolved. Russian money reportedly went to European politicians through Voice of Europe, a network operating in the Czech Republic. The Czech government put it, Viktor Medvedchuk and Artyom Marchevsky on its sanctions list in March 2024. Czech counter-intelligence said the money came from Russia. Payments reportedly went to politicians in Belgium, France, Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Poland. President Miloš Zeman made Ye Jianming his economic adviser while Ye's company CEFC bought Czech assets. Ye had been deputy head of CAIFC, a Chinese state 'friendship' body. China detained Ye in 2018. Older history includes the 1939 transfer of 23 tons of Czechoslovak gold to Nazi Germany's central bank by the Bank for International Settlements. Václav Klaus, prime minister and later president, is a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market forum. No finding says it directed his decisions.
Czech Republic.imp: Czech taxpayers fund EU farm subsidies, and the EU audit found the prime minister controlled a company receiving them. Ministers decide rules that affect his business. Russian money reportedly went to candidates through a network based in the country, which affects how Czech and European voters are informed before elections. A Chinese company bought Czech assets while its chairman advised the president.

Denmark.d: Denmark's military intelligence service, FE, let the US National Security Agency tap internet cables passing through Danish intercept stations such as Sandagergård. An internal review called Operation Dunhammer found the NSA used this access in 2012–2014 to wiretap Germany's chancellor, Angela Merkel, and other German politicians. It also reportedly targeted senior figures in Sweden, Norway and France. Danish media made this public in 2021, and the FE chief and three other officials were suspended. In Greenland, a self-governing part of Denmark, Danish police intelligence confirmed in 2025 that an influence campaign was under way. Danish media reported that at least three Americans, said to have ties to the Trump administration, tried to stir anti-Danish feeling there. Danske Bank pleaded guilty in a US court in 2022 to bank fraud conspiracy. About €200 billion from non-resident clients had moved through its Estonian branch. It forfeited $2 billion. The world's largest container lines carry multi-tonne cocaine loads without being charged, because shore crews load and unload the drugs without their knowledge. King Frederik X is an alumnus of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme. During the Cold War, Denmark's secret stay-behind network, called Absalon, was hidden inside military intelligence. Denmark disbanded it after Italy's 1990 disclosure of Gladio.
Denmark.imp: Danish intelligence let a foreign agency use Danish cables to listen to allied leaders, which damages trust with neighbouring countries. Greenlanders face a reported foreign campaign aimed at turning them against Denmark. Danish customers and shareholders saw their bank used to move dirty money and pay a $2 billion penalty. Residents have few ways to learn what their own intelligence service shares.

Estonia.d: Azerbaijan's ruling elite moved about $2.9 billion through Danske Bank's branch in Tallinn in 2012–2014, using four UK shell companies. Leaked records published in 2017 showed almost half came from an account linked to the Aliyev family at the International Bank of Azerbaijan. Some of the money reached European politicians, including German MP Karin Strenz, and people who defended Azerbaijan in the Council of Europe's assembly. In 2018 the European Central Bank withdrew the licence of Versobank, a small Estonian bank, for serious failures to stop money laundering. Most of its clients were non-residents. The Estonian church of the Moscow Patriarchate, part of the Russian Orthodox Church, has about 150,000 faithful. In 2024 Estonia refused to renew its head's residence permit, calling his support for Russia's war a security risk. Parliament then declared the Moscow Patriarchate an institution that supports Russian aggression. In 2025 it changed the law to limit foreign control of churches. Kaja Kallas, then prime minister, is on the official 2024 list of the Bilderberg meeting, a private conference of politicians and executives. She has been the EU's foreign policy chief since December 2024. Economy minister Erkki Keldo joined the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders in 2025.
Estonia.imp: Banks in Tallinn were used to move billions for foreign elites, and supervisors closed one small bank over money laundering. Orthodox believers in the Moscow Patriarchate church have seen their leader expelled and their church declared to support Russian aggression. Residents cannot learn what their then prime minister discussed at a private meeting, because Bilderberg keeps no public record.

Finland.d: President Alexander Stubb is listed as a member of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leader network since 2009. The WEF, which runs the annual Davos meeting, picks people under 40 for this programme. Stubb also appears on the official lists of the Bilderberg meeting for 2024 and 2025, both times as sitting head of state. Bilderberg is a private yearly conference of about 130 politicians, executives and academics, with no public record of what is said. Former prime minister Sanna Marin is also listed as a Young Global Leader alumna, and she is on the 2025 Bilderberg list. Membership of these forums is lawful, and no finding says they directed Finnish government decisions. After the 1944 armistice with the Soviet Union, army officers hid weapons across the country for up to 35,000 men. Between 5,000 and 10,000 people took part. Under a 1947 law, 1,488 people were convicted, most receiving one to four months in prison. Finland is in the Minimal band for organised crime.
Finland.imp: Finnish voters know their president and a former prime minister attend private forums with business leaders. They cannot learn what was discussed there, because these meetings keep no public record. No case shows these contacts changed Finnish policy. No documented case shows criminal groups paying Finnish police or courts. Bilderberg does publish its participant lists, so residents can see who attends.

France.d: In Marseille, officers of the northern anti-crime brigade were convicted of stealing seized cannabis, cash and phones from the estates they policed. A former head of the national anti-drug office is under formal investigation over cannabis shipments that moved by way of an informer; he denies wrongdoing. Morocco was linked to the selection of President Macron's phone number for Pegasus spyware in 2021, which Morocco denies. In 2024 the interior minister accused Azerbaijan of stirring unrest in New Caledonia; Azerbaijan denied it. Russia's First Czech Russian Bank lent the Front National €9 million in 2014. The Uber Files suggest Macron, as economy minister, helped Uber against cabinet opponents. A Senate inquiry found state use of consultants such as McKinsey shaped policy, and prosecutors are investigating McKinsey for tax fraud. In 2021 a court convicted drug maker Servier over Mediator and fined the medicines agency for failing to act. Macron was a Rothschild partner before joining the Élysée in 2012. Some claim Rothschild directs French policy; this is an antisemitic conspiracy theory, and no evidence supports it. A 2025 government report said the Muslim Brotherhood seeks influence in local councils. Older history includes Freemason files used to block army promotions in 1904 and CIA funding of the Paris-based Congress for Cultural Freedom.
France.imp: Residents of Marseille's northern estates were robbed by the police officers sent to protect them. Patients took Mediator for years while the regulator failed to act on warnings, and it is thought to have caused 500 to 2,000 deaths. Taxpayers paid consultants whose advice shaped policy without public scrutiny. Voters have a major party that borrowed from a Russian bank. People cannot easily tell whether a decision came from ministers or from a firm lobbying them.

Germany.d: Former chancellor Gerhard Schröder chaired the shareholders' committee of Nord Stream, which built Russia's Baltic gas pipelines, and later chaired the board of Rosneft, a Russian state oil company. In 2022 the Bundestag closed his former-chancellor's office. Munich prosecutors are investigating AfD politician Petr Bystron over cash reportedly handed over by Voice of Europe, a Russian-funded network based in Prague. He denies it and has not been charged. Jan Marsalek, chief operating officer of the Munich payments firm Wirecard until its collapse in 2020, is wanted by German police. Investigators say he had worked with Russian intelligence since at least 2010. In 2025 a Dresden court jailed Jian Guo, an aide to AfD MEP Maximilian Krah, for spying for China's Ministry of State Security. Three Germans are on trial in Düsseldorf, charged with passing naval technology to the same ministry. In 2021 the Bundestag lifted the immunity of two CDU MPs accused of taking money to lobby for Azerbaijan. Turkey's state religious authority trains and pays the imams of DITIB, which runs about 900 mosques in Germany. A 2017 inquiry into DITIB imams spying for Ankara was dropped for lack of evidence. In Hamburg and Bremerhaven, courts have convicted customs officers and port workers of clearing cocaine containers. Chancellor Friedrich Merz chaired BlackRock's German arm until 2020, and Jörg Kukies moved from Goldman Sachs to the finance ministry and chancellery. Earlier, the CIA paid for Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty in Munich until the early 1970s. The BND intelligence service ran a secret NATO stay-behind network until the government ordered it dissolved in 1991.
Germany.imp: People in Germany who criticise Beijing or Moscow share the country with people those governments recruited, as the Guo and Marsalek cases showed. Wirecard investors and reporters saw the financial regulator ban short-selling and file complaints against the Financial Times journalists who exposed the fraud. A study found that the federal risk agency copied industry text into its glyphosate safety review, which the EU used to approve the weedkiller that farmers and gardeners still use.

Greece.d: In 2001, as Greece joined the euro, Goldman Sachs arranged currency swaps that worked as a hidden loan of about €2.8 billion. Greece paid Goldman fees, and its debt under the deal grew to €5.1 billion. Lucas Papademos ran the Bank of Greece when the swaps were made. In 2011 he was installed as unelected prime minister to secure the second EU–IMF bailout. Lazard, a US-French investment bank, advised the government on the 2012 bond swap and was hired again by Syriza in 2015. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis attended the private Bilderberg conference in 2025 while in office. In 2018 prosecutors alleged that the Swiss drug company Novartis bribed Greek officials, naming two former prime ministers. Those named denied it, and the cases against them were dropped. In 2020 Novartis settled US charges that included bribing Greek hospital staff and doctors. At Piraeus, part of a heroin load from the tanker Noor 1 disappeared before police secured it, and its operators were convicted. In Attica in 2012, polling stations used by police officers gave Golden Dawn just over a fifth of the vote. In 2020 an Athens court convicted the party's leaders of running a criminal organisation. Members of IDEA, an officers' society formed in 1945, led the 1967 coup, and a NATO stay-behind unit took over the Defence Ministry that day. Greece's stay-behind branch, Operation Sheepskin, ran until 1988.
Greece.imp: Greeks carried the fees and the growing debt from the Goldman swaps, which official figures did not show until 2010. The second bailout was secured by a prime minister whom no voter had chosen. Migrants lived with Golden Dawn, whose leaders were convicted of running a criminal organisation, while many Athens police officers voted for it. Patients were treated in hospitals where, according to US charges that Novartis settled, the company paid staff and doctors.

Hungary.d: In February 2024 Interior Minister Sándor Pintér reached a policing agreement with China's Minister of Public Security. It lets Chinese police officers patrol with Hungarian police in tourist areas and at large events. Safeguard Defenders, a human-rights group, listed two Chinese police 'service stations' in Budapest, in the Józsefváros and Kőbánya districts. The interior ministry denies that any such stations exist. Béla Kovács sat in the European Parliament for Jobbik, a Hungarian nationalist party. Prosecutors accused him of spying on EU institutions for Russia. In 2022 Hungary's top court, the Curia, sentenced him in absentia to five years in prison. He lives in Russia. Opus Dei, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, the Legion of Christ and Israel's foreign intelligence service, Mossad, are recorded as present in Hungary, without a documented case. The Trilateral Commission and the Mont Pelerin Society, two private forums for politicians and business, also have members there. Hungary is in the High band and scores 7.5 out of 10 for officials acting for outside interests. Older history includes Radio Free Europe, which the CIA paid for until the early 1970s and which broadcast from Munich into the Soviet bloc.
Hungary.imp: Hungarians, and Chinese people living in Hungary, can meet Chinese officers on patrol in tourist areas and at large events, under an agreement their own government signed. Chinese residents who oppose Beijing may meet officers who answer to China's public security ministry. Voters who elected Kovács to the European Parliament were represented by a man the Curia later found had spied for Russia.

Iceland.d: No case of outside forces placing people or money in Iceland's government is documented yet, so this account is a best guess. Iceland is in the Minimal band. It scores 1.0 out of 10 for officials acting for outside interests and 8.2 for its courts, police and watchdogs. The Mont Pelerin Society, a private forum of free-market economists and politicians, has documented members there. The company Samherji is headquartered in Iceland. A NATO stay-behind network, which other member states ran in secret during the Cold War, is likely to have existed but is not documented.
Iceland.imp: On present evidence, people in Iceland face little risk that officials act for foreign states, criminal groups or companies. Its courts, police and watchdogs score well. Because no case has been documented, any outside influence that exists has not been tested in a court or an inquiry, and residents cannot know its size.

Ireland.d: In September 2022 Safeguard Defenders, a human-rights group, reported a Chinese police 'service station' on Capel Street in Dublin, run for the police of the city of Fuzhou. Such stations were used to pressure people wanted by China to go back. In October 2022 Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs ordered it to close. The World Economic Forum named Leo Varadkar to its 2018 class of Young Global Leaders, a network for people under about 40, while he was Taoiseach. In 2024, weeks after he stepped down, he was on the official list for the Bilderberg conference. Simon Harris joined the 2025 class while he was Tánaiste, foreign minister and defence minister. Membership of these forums is lawful and no finding shows that they directed government decisions. Opus Dei, the Legion of Christ, Tradition, Family, Property and Uber are recorded as present in Ireland. Ireland is in the Low band. Older history left the Knights of Saint Columbanus, a Catholic men's order. Taoiseach John A. Costello and other members of his 1948 cabinet were Knights, according to biographers. His government gave Maynooth seminary a special yearly grant. Justice Minister Seán MacEoin, also a Knight, reportedly assured the Order's council that the government would avoid conflict between Church and State. Members also held civil-service posts, including Dublin City's chief planner.
Ireland.imp: Chinese people in Ireland wanted by Beijing could be pressed to go back through a station run for Fuzhou police, until the state closed it in 2022. Voters who elect a Taoiseach or Tánaiste cannot see what is said at Bilderberg, where no public record is kept. In 1948 a justice minister who was a Knight reported to the Order's council. Labour's William Davin, a Knight, is reported to have worked against the Mother and Child health scheme.

Italy.d: Since 1991 Italy's government has dissolved town councils and health authorities 402 times after finding mafia groups controlled them. Calabria, Campania and Sicily account for 360 of those decrees. In Calabria the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, has controlled hiring and container handling at the port of Gioia Tauro. Former senator Giancarlo Pittelli was convicted in 2023 of collusion with its Mancuso clan. In Emilia-Romagna, the top court confirmed in 2022 that a 'Ndrangheta clan ran and took over construction firms. Salvatore Cuffaro, President of Sicily until 2008, was jailed for aiding Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian mafia. Nicola Cosentino, a former economy undersecretary, was convicted of protecting the Casalesi clan of the Camorra, the Naples mafia. In Sicily's Nebrodi mountains, two clans claimed EU farm subsidies on land they controlled, and the top court made the convictions final. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini's Lega has a cooperation pact with Vladimir Putin's United Russia party, renewed to 2027. Luca Volontè, a former Italian MP, was jailed for taking Azerbaijani money to vote in the Council of Europe's assembly. Qu Dongyu, a former Chinese vice-minister, heads the UN food agency FAO in Rome. Mario Draghi, vice chairman of Goldman Sachs International until 2005, and Mario Monti, a former Goldman adviser, both later served as prime minister. Older history left the P2 Masonic lodge, whose seized 1981 list named the heads of all three intelligence services. Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti disclosed Gladio, a secret NATO stay-behind force, in 1990. Courts later called P2's head, Licio Gelli, the financier of the 1980 Bologna station bombing.
Italy.imp: In hundreds of towns in Calabria, Campania and Sicily, residents have had their elected councils removed and replaced by commissioners for up to two years. Firms tied to clans have bid for public building work paid with EU recovery funds, and in 2024 the Reggio Emilia prefect barred 80 of them. EU farm money meant for farmers in the Nebrodi went to clan members. The families of the 85 people killed in the Bologna bombing waited decades for courts to name who paid for it.

Latvia.d:
Tatjana Ždanoka, co-chair of the Latvian Russian Union party, sat in the European Parliament for Latvia from 2004 to 2024. Leaked emails published in January 2024 by The Insider and partner outlets showed her reporting to officers of Russia's FSB security service from at least 2004. Latvia's State Security Service opened a criminal case in February 2024 and searched her property that July. The European Parliament penalised her for breaking its code of conduct. She has not been convicted.

In 2018 FinCEN, the US Treasury's anti-laundering unit, named ABLV Bank a primary money-laundering concern. Depositors withdrew their money and the bank wound itself up within weeks, without a trial. In 2021 the US sanctioned Chatex, a crypto exchange with supporting companies in Latvia and Estonia, as a successor to an exchange it had already sanctioned. Money from Russia's Global Laundromat scheme also passed through Latvian banks.

Until 2022 the Latvian Orthodox Church was a self-governing part of the Russian Orthodox Church, which answers to the Patriarch in Moscow. In September 2022 parliament passed a bill from President Egils Levits making the church independent of any authority outside Latvia. The President's office must now be told when its bishops are appointed. No Orthodox church had recognised the new status by mid-2026. Opus Dei and the Order of Malta, two Catholic bodies, also have a documented presence; membership is lawful.
Latvia.imp: Latvian voters elected a member of the European Parliament who, according to leaked emails, reported to Russian intelligence for twenty years; a criminal case is open. ABLV's customers saw their bank close within weeks of a US decision, with no court hearing. Orthodox believers in Latvia now belong to a church that is legally separate from Moscow but that no other Orthodox church had recognised by mid-2026.

Liechtenstein.d: Nothing is documented yet for Liechtenstein, so this is a best guess. No case has been recorded of a foreign state, criminal group or company paying officials or placing people in its government, courts or firms. The only listed organisation with a documented presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic religious order; membership is lawful. Liechtenstein is in the Minimal band of the Global Organized Crime Index. The index gives it 1.0 of 10 for officials acting for outside interests and 8.4 of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. A case may exist that no court or published investigation has yet described.
Liechtenstein.imp: No cost to residents has been documented. The index scores suggest that officials seldom act for outside interests and that courts, police and watchdogs work as intended. If that changes, residents would most likely learn of it through a court case, a regulator's decision or a published investigation. That is how such cases have come to light in neighbouring countries.

Lithuania.d:
A group selling cocaine, MDMA, ketamine and methamphetamine in Iceland laundered its income through real estate in Lithuania. Police in five countries arrested 24 people in February 2026; the suspects are charged, not convicted. In December 2024 French and Dutch investigators shut Matrix, an invitation-only encrypted phone network that ran on more than 40 servers. They had read 2.3 million of its messages over three months. It was found on the phone of a man convicted of murdering a Dutch crime journalist.

In 2002 Yuri Borisov, a Russian businessman who ran the helicopter firm Avia Baltika, reportedly gave about 400,000 dollars to Rolandas Paksas's presidential campaign. After Paksas won, he granted Borisov Lithuanian citizenship by decree. The Constitutional Court found that Paksas had broken the constitution and his oath. In April 2004 the Seimas, Lithuania's parliament, removed him, the first European head of state to be impeached. The European Court of Human Rights later found his lifetime ban from parliament disproportionate.

Opus Dei, the Order of Malta and Tradition, Family, Property, a Catholic traditionalist movement, have a documented presence. So does the Atlas Network of free-market think tanks. No case connects them to wrongdoing in Lithuania.
Lithuania.imp: Lithuanian homes and land have been bought with money from drug sales in Iceland, so ordinary buyers compete with laundered cash. In 2004 Lithuanians saw their president removed after a foreign donor who had funded his campaign received citizenship from him. A court case showed that a president's decree could be paid for. Lithuania's own constitutional court and parliament dealt with the case and removed him.

Luxembourg.d:
Between May 1984 and April 1986, 18 bombs went off in Luxembourg, many at power pylons. In 2013 two former members of the Gendarmerie's mobile brigade, Jos Wilmes and Marc Scheer, went on trial for them. Their defence argued that NATO's Stay Behind network, a secret armed reserve set up to resist an invasion, carried out the attacks. A 2006 recording was played in court of Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, the justice minister and the intelligence chief speculating about Stay Behind involvement. The prosecutor said 88 of 125 pieces of evidence had disappeared. The trial was suspended in 2014.

Eight former gendarmerie and police officers were later sent to trial for false testimony, but not for the bombings. No court has found who planted the bombs or that Stay Behind was involved.

Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), a bank that carried hidden money for many clients, was registered in Luxembourg and run from London. Regulators in several countries closed it in July 1991. Le Cercle and the Trilateral Commission, two private forums of politicians and business leaders, also have a documented presence. Luxembourg is in the Minimal band of the Global Organized Crime Index.
Luxembourg.imp: Four decades later, Luxembourg residents still do not know who bombed their power lines and public sites in the 1980s. Evidence went missing while it was in state hands, so the case may never be resolved. BCCI's customers in Luxembourg lost access to their bank when regulators closed it in 1991.

Malta.d:
Yorgen Fenech, a Maltese businessman, owned 17 Black, a company registered in the United Arab Emirates. He was also a director of Electrogas, which built Malta's gas power station under a state contract. Leaked papers showed that Panama companies belonging to Keith Schembri, the prime minister's chief of staff, and energy minister Konrad Mizzi expected payments from 17 Black. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating these companies when a car bomb killed her in 2017. Fenech is charged with complicity in her murder, and his trial began in mid-2026. In February 2025 he, Mizzi and Schembri were charged with corruption over the Electrogas project. A 2021 public inquiry found the state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'.

Italian investigators found Calabrian and Sicilian mafia groups using Malta-licensed online betting firms to collect bets and launder money. The Malta Gaming Authority suspended several licences after a 2018 Palermo operation. Some executives were later acquitted.

Pilatus Bank lost its Maltese licence in 2018 after its owner was arrested in the United States. He was convicted of evading Iran sanctions through the bank, but the conviction was later vacated. The US sanctioned Maltese, Libyan and Egyptian brokers in 2018 for smuggling Libyan oil to Europe. Two crypto exchanges linked to Malta, Binance and OKX, pleaded guilty in the US to anti-laundering and licensing offences. The European Court of Justice ruled against Malta's scheme that sold citizenship for investment.

Malta's failure to act on early warnings about Pilatus helped put it on the FATF grey list in 2021. FATF is the international body that sets anti-laundering rules.
Malta.imp: Maltese taxpayers fund a power station built under a contract that, prosecutors say, was linked to payments meant for a minister and the prime minister's chief of staff. A journalist who reported on it was killed. The 2021 grey listing told foreign banks to treat money from Malta as higher risk. Maltese citizenship, with the EU rights that come with it, was offered for sale under a scheme the European Court of Justice ruled against.

Moldova.d:
Between 2010 and 2014 Russian companies moved an estimated $20–80 billion out of Russia through Moldova. They signed fake debts, and Moldovan judges ordered the debts paid into Moldindconbank and on through Latvian banks. Moldovan prosecutors later charged judges who had approved the debts. This scheme is known as the Global Laundromat.

In 2014 about $1 billion, equal to 12% of Moldova's GDP, was taken from three Moldovan banks. The money left through loans that were repaid with new loans and passed through UK and Hong Kong shell companies. Vlad Plahotniuc led the Democratic Party and was widely described as controlling the government and parliament. He fled in 2019 and was arrested in Greece in 2025. In April 2026 a Chișinău court sentenced him to 19 years.

In June 2023 Moldova's Constitutional Court banned the Șor Party of businessman Ilan Shor for serving a foreign state's interests. Evghenia Guțul won the governorship of Gagauzia, an autonomous region, as its candidate and met Vladimir Putin in 2024. In August 2025 a court sentenced her to seven years for financing the party with undeclared Russian money. The party's former secretary was sentenced for paying protesters.

In 2018 Moldova's Security and Intelligence Service detained seven Turkish teachers and managers from Orizont, a Gülen-linked school chain, and sent them to Turkey. In 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that this was an illegal transfer and ordered compensation for each of them.
Moldova.imp: The 2014 bank theft took money equal to about an eighth of everything Moldova produces in a year. Judges approved fake debts for foreign clients, so residents cannot assume a court ruling reflects the law. Voters in Gagauzia elected a governor whose campaign party, a court found, was financed with undeclared Russian money. Turkish families in Moldova learned that the security service could hand them to Ankara without a lawful process.

Monaco.d:
France proposes or supplies several of Monaco's top officials. The prince consults the French government before choosing the head of government, called the Minister of State. Christophe Mirmand, a senior French civil servant, has held that post since July 2025. French magistrates proposed by Paris hold key judicial posts, a French officer commands the police, and France is responsible for Monaco's defence. Until 2002 the Minister of State had to be a French citizen picked from names Paris put forward. Treaties and Monaco's constitution set out these arrangements.

World Athletics, the governing body of the sport, is based in Monaco. Its former president, Lamine Diack, was convicted in Paris in 2020 of taking money to hide Russian athletes' doping. About €3.2 million was extorted from suspected dopers so they could compete at the London Olympics. Investigators found he agreed a $1.5 million deal with Russian sports officials to fund a presidential campaign in Senegal. He died with appeals pending.

Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns AS Monaco football club, was made a suspect in 2018 in a corruption case over his contacts with Monaco officials. A complaint also named a former public prosecutor. Monaco's courts closed the case in February 2025, ruling that the phone evidence had been obtained unlawfully.
Monaco.imp: Monaco residents are governed, judged and policed partly by officials chosen with the French government, under treaties Monaco signed. Athletes who competed clean raced against Russian dopers while the sport's governing body in Monaco took money to delay cases. The Rybolovlev case ended on how the evidence was collected, so residents have no court finding either way on whether officials were influenced.

Montenegro.d:
In January 2026 the High Court in Podgorica sentenced Vesna Medenica, president of the Supreme Court until 2020, to 10 years. It found she used her position to protect a cigarette and narcotics smuggling network led by her son Miloš. He was sentenced to just over 10 years but fled while under house arrest. The evidence included decrypted messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service used by criminal groups.

Sky ECC messages passed on by Europol also led to charges over protection of the Kavac clan's cocaine trade. Those charged include a former chief special prosecutor, a former assistant police director and his son, a state security officer. Separate indictments name another former Supreme Court president, two former police directors and the mayor of Budva. These are charges, not convictions.

Prime Minister Milojko Spajić was named to the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders class of 2025. The programme is a five-year series of meetings and courses run by the Davos forum for people under about 40. Being selected is not wrongdoing.

The Japanese religious group Aum Shinrikyo, now called Aleph, has a documented presence, as does the Order of Malta, a Catholic order. Montenegro is in the High band of the Global Organized Crime Index.
Montenegro.imp: People in Montenegro who went to court could not assume their case was heard fairly when the head of the Supreme Court was protecting her son's smuggling business. Prosecutors and police commanders charged with protecting a cocaine clan were the officials meant to investigate it. Residents now depend on messages decrypted abroad, rather than on their own institutions, for evidence against senior officials.

Netherlands.d:
At the port of Rotterdam, terminal employees and IT contractors were convicted of giving cocaine smugglers PIN codes for the port's container release system. In July 2023 customs found 8 tonnes of cocaine in a banana shipment there, the largest seizure in Dutch history. Inez Weski, lawyer for drug boss Ridouan Taghi, was convicted in May 2026 of taking part in his organisation by passing his messages out of prison. Earlier in Taghi's Marengo trial, a lawyer and a police employee were prosecuted for leaking protected information to his network.

In The Hague, Dutch military intelligence caught four Russian GRU officers in 2018 trying to hack the chemical weapons watchdog, the OPCW. In 2024 journalists reported that Israeli intelligence spied on and pressured International Criminal Court staff for nearly ten years; Israel denied it. In 2025 a former ASML and NXP engineer was jailed for sending chip-making files to a contact in Russia. That year the government took control of chipmaker Nexperia from its partly state-owned Chinese owner, Wingtech, then suspended the order. In 2022 the foreign minister ordered two Chinese 'police stations' shut.

Memos showed that Shell and Unilever lobbied for the 2017 plan to scrap the dividend tax, which no party had campaigned for. A 2020 parliamentary inquiry found Saudi, Kuwaiti, Emirati and Qatari donors funding mosques and influencing the choice of imams. ING and ABN AMRO paid €775 million and €480 million to settle laundering-control failures. King Willem-Alexander is on the 2024 and 2025 lists for Bilderberg, a private yearly conference of politicians and executives.

A secret NATO stay-behind network operated from 1945 to 1992; the government acknowledged it to relatives in 2021.
Netherlands.imp: Rotterdam residents live beside a port where cocaine gangs have bribed workers, and violence has followed: a witness's brother, his lawyer and a journalist were murdered around the Marengo trial. Taxpayers paid to harden prisons against escape plots. Mosque-goers may hear imams chosen with foreign donors' money. European carmakers faced chip shortages when China blocked Nexperia exports in response to the Dutch order.

Norway.d:
Eirik Jensen ran the Oslo police narcotics section for years. In 2020 an appeal court convicted him of aggravated corruption and of helping an informant he managed import about fourteen tonnes of hashish. He was sentenced to twenty-one years. The Supreme Court refused his appeal in 2021. It is the most senior conviction of a police officer for this kind of offence in Scandinavia.

Norway had a secret stay-behind network, part of NATO planning for armed resistance after an invasion. In 1978 police found weapons and radio equipment at a mountain cabin and arrested businessman Hans Otto Meyer. He said Norwegian intelligence had supplied them. Defence Minister Rolf Hansen then said the network did not answer to NATO and had no CIA connection. In 1957 Norway's intelligence chief, Vilhelm Evang, had protested to NATO about stay-behind activity by officers at its Kolsås headquarters. NATO gave assurances in 1958 on how the networks would be run.

Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation, has a documented presence. So do the Trilateral Commission, a private forum of politicians and business leaders, the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market academic society, and Alp Services, a private intelligence firm. No case connects them to wrongdoing in Norway. Norway is in the Minimal band of the Global Organized Crime Index.
Norway.imp: For years the officer in charge of fighting drugs in Oslo was helping an informant bring hashish into the city. Drug cases his section handled in that period may have been shaped by that arrangement. In 1978 Norwegians learned that weapons supplied by their own intelligence service were hidden in a mountain cabin. The index scores suggest such cases are rare today.

Poland.d:
Ordo Iuris is a conservative Catholic legal institute based in Poland. Its co-founder, Aleksander Stępkowski, was made deputy foreign minister by the new Law and Justice government in 2015. In 2016 Ordo Iuris drafted a near-total abortion ban, which parliament rejected after national protests. Stępkowski was appointed to the Supreme Court in 2019 with no previous experience as a judge. In May 2020 President Andrzej Duda made him acting First President of the court.

In 2019 police arrested Wang Weijing, a senior Huawei employee in Poland, and Piotr Durbajło, a former Internal Security Agency officer. Prosecutors charged both with working for Chinese intelligence. They say Wang sought contracts that would give Huawei insight into state and local government data systems. Both pleaded not guilty, and the trial in Warsaw has been closed to the public.

Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski is on the 2024 and 2025 lists for Bilderberg, a private yearly conference of politicians and executives. Finance minister Andrzej Domański was on the 2024 list. Przemysław Wipler, a Confederation member of parliament elected in 2023, was reported to be an Opus Dei supernumerary, a lay member. Attending a forum or belonging to Opus Dei is lawful.

In June 2026 police arrested 20 people over a methamphetamine trade that used a hub at Rzeszów to move drugs from Western Europe to Slovakia and western Ukraine.
Poland.imp: Poles who go to the Supreme Court may have their case heard under a judge appointed without judicial experience, who had co-founded a conservative legal institute. Women's access to abortion was the subject of a draft law written by that institute. If the Huawei charges are proven, contracts paid for by Polish taxpayers would have given a foreign intelligence service access to public data.

Portugal.d:
Ricardo Salgado led Banco Espírito Santo, a family bank tied to Portuguese governments since the Salazar dictatorship. The bank collapsed in 2014. In Operation Marquês, prosecutors charged former Prime Minister José Sócrates with taking undue payments, including money they link to the Espírito Santo group. Salgado faces three counts of corruption and eight of money laundering. A judge threw out most charges, an appeal court reinstated them, and the trial began in July 2025. All defendants are presumed innocent.

Between the Canaries and the Azores, cocaine smugglers use large ships to carry cargo from Latin America into international waters. They pass it to fast boats, which then land it on remote Portuguese and Spanish coastline. In April 2026 a Spanish-led operation seized 11 tonnes of cocaine, intercepted eight vessels and arrested 54 people.

The World Economic Forum named José Manuel Durão Barroso a Global Leader for Tomorrow in 1993, when he was foreign minister. He later became prime minister and then president of the European Commission. Selection is not a finding of influence.

Under the Salazar dictatorship, a group called Aginter Press was set up in Lisbon in 1966. It called itself a news agency but trained members in bombing and sabotage. An Italian magistrate told his parliament's terrorism commission that Aginter instructors taught Italian neo-fascists to use explosives. Its leaders left Portugal after the 1974 revolution.
Portugal.imp: Banco Espírito Santo's collapse in 2014 hit the people who had their savings and shares in it. Portuguese voters are still waiting for a court to decide whether a former prime minister took money linked to the bank's owners. Until then, the charges remain unproven. People on remote stretches of the Portuguese coast live where boats carrying cocaine come ashore at night.

Romania.d:
In September 2019 Newsweek România reported, citing unnamed Masonic sources, that two senior security officials were Freemasons. They were Mihai Fifor, then interim interior minister and deputy prime minister, and General Constantin Florea, head of the Gendarmerie, a military police force. Neither had declared membership in his interest declaration, which the magazine said the law required. Fifor neither confirmed nor denied it. Costin Mihalache, head of the Government Chancellery and a former foreign-intelligence officer, said he had been a Mason but no longer was. The claim rests on that one outlet, and Masonic membership is lawful.

In February 2026 French and Romanian police arrested 13 people in a network that laundered 306 million euros of drug and tax-evasion money. It issued invoices between the two countries for services never performed. Each false invoice moved money and reduced taxable income. The money then went into front companies and real estate.

Opus Dei, the Order of Malta, the Trilateral Commission and Radio Free Europe, a US-funded broadcaster, have a documented presence. So does Azerbaijan's lobbying operation known as 'caviar diplomacy'. No case connects any of them to wrongdoing in Romania.
Romania.imp: Romanians cannot check whether the officials in charge of their police belong to private lodges, because the declarations meant to show this did not mention it. Laundered drug money entered Romanian property, so ordinary buyers competed with it. False invoices cut the taxes owed, which reduces the money available for schools, hospitals and roads.

Russia.d:
Bank Rossiya in St Petersburg was refounded by businessmen who later shared a dacha cooperative with Vladimir Putin. The US Treasury calls it 'the personal bank for senior officials' and has sanctioned it since 2014. A 2023 presidential decree let the state take 'temporary management' of foreign companies' Russian assets. The state property agency then took over Danone's Russian business and Carlsberg's Baltika brewery. Yakub Zakriev, Chechnya's agriculture minister and a nephew of Ramzan Kadyrov, became head of Danone Russia. In 2019 the FSB, Russia's security service, arrested American investor Michael Calvey during a shareholder dispute; his conviction was vacated in 2024.

In Kushchyovskaya, in Krasnodar region, a gang that local police and officials had protected for years murdered 12 people in 2010. In Moscow, five drug squad officers were convicted in 2022 of planting drugs on a journalist.

Reports for the World Anti-Doping Agency found that the sports ministry and the FSB ran a doping cover-up, including at the 2014 Sochi Olympics. Since 2022 Interpol checks each Russian alert before passing it on. Crypto exchanges such as Garantex keep operating from Moscow after US sanctions.

Abroad, Russia funds the Russkiy Mir Foundation, and the Czech government sanctioned the Voice of Europe network in 2024 for paying European politicians. Russia banned the US-funded National Endowment for Democracy in 2015; no independent body has found that it worked inside Russian institutions.

Alexander Kerensky, prime minister of the 1917 Provisional Government, led the Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples, a Masonic lodge. A claim that banker Jacob Schiff financed the Bolsheviks is an antisemitic myth; Kuhn, Loeb records show he refused them aid.
Russia.imp: Russian business owners can lose a company to officials' friends through a decree or an arrest. Residents of Kushchyovskaya lived for years under a gang the local police protected. Athletes worldwide competed against Russians protected by the state doping cover-up. Russians abroad can be targeted through Interpol requests, though checks now limit this.

San Marino.d:
According to prosecutors, construction and banking entrepreneurs paid San Marino politicians to obtain building permits and banking licences. The cash came from an account in the name of 'Giuseppe Mazzini' at Banca Commerciale Sammarinese, so the case is known as Conto Mazzini. Twenty-one former political figures went on trial in 2015 for criminal association to launder bribes. They included former state secretaries Fiorenzo Stolfi and Claudio Podeschi; state secretaries are San Marino's government ministers. About 200 million euros was seized. Several defendants were convicted in 2017. In March 2022 an appeal court upheld most of the convictions and reduced the sentences.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic religious order, also has a documented presence; membership is lawful. San Marino is in the Moderate band of the Global Organized Crime Index. The index gives it 5.0 of 10 for officials acting for outside interests and 5.3 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.
San Marino.imp: In San Marino, building permits and banking licences went to those who paid politicians, according to the courts. Builders and bankers who did not pay competed against firms that had bought their approvals. Residents lived with buildings and banks approved this way. The 2022 appeal ruling confirmed most convictions, so several former ministers have been held to account.

Serbia.d:
Members of the Belivuk-Miljković criminal group held state security identity cards and had access to protected facilities, according to evidence in their prosecution. A former head of the security service was later charged in connection with them. The case is still running, and who is responsible remains disputed in Serbian politics.

In 2003 Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić was shot by a serving commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, the JSO. The unit had merged with the Zemun criminal clan, which held a share of the Balkan heroin trade. Twelve people were convicted in 2007, and the unit was disbanded.

In 1903 army officers led by Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, killed King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga. Apis and fellow officers later founded the secret society Unification or Death, called the Black Hand, and he became chief of army intelligence. Many scholars hold that he approved the 1914 assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo.

He was shot in 1917 after a court-martial for treason, and Serbia's Supreme Court acquitted him in 1953. A rival officers' group, the White Hand, backed King Alexander I when he suspended the constitution. Its leader, General Petar Živković, then became prime minister.
Serbia.imp: Serbians elected a prime minister who was killed by an officer of their own state's special police unit working with a criminal clan. A criminal group carrying state security identity cards could pass checks meant to protect the public. Until the courts finish the Belivuk case, residents do not know how many security officials helped it.

Slovakia.d:
Journalist Ján Kuciak and his fiancée Martina Kušnírová were shot dead in February 2018. His unfinished article described Italian businessmen running farm companies in eastern Slovakia, including Antonino Vadalà. Vadalà had been named in Italian investigations into the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia. The article showed that Mária Trošková, chief state adviser to Prime Minister Robert Fico, had co-founded a company with Vadalà in 2011. Trošková and Security Council secretary Viliam Jasaň stepped down, saying their names were being misused. Fico resigned in March 2018 after mass protests. No court has found that the prime minister's office acted for the 'Ndrangheta.

In July 2017 Trinh Xuan Thanh, a former Vietnamese state-company executive seeking asylum, was seized in Berlin. Germany blamed Vietnamese intelligence, and a Berlin court jailed one accomplice. In 2019 a Slovak journalist found an invoice from Slovakia's interior ministry to Vietnam's for a government flight to Moscow three days after the abduction. Former president Andrej Kiska wrote that then interior minister Robert Kaliňák arranged the loan of the plane. Thanh was later given a life sentence in Hanoi.
