Agrofert, an agricultural and food company, has a documented presence, as do the Atlas Network of free-market think tanks and Radio Free Europe.
Slovakia.imp: Slovaks lost a journalist who was investigating businessmen with suspected mafia links and their ties to the prime minister's office. A Slovak government plane, paid for by taxpayers, was reportedly used to move a kidnapped man toward a life sentence in Vietnam. What residents know about who approved the flight comes from a former president's account and an invoice, not from a court.

Slovenia.d:
Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, signed a 278 million euro deal in 2006 to sell Slovenia 135 armoured vehicles. In 2008 Finnish broadcaster YLE alleged that Patria paid bribes, partly aimed at Prime Minister Janez Janša, to win the deal. A Ljubljana court sentenced Janša to two years in prison in 2013.

The Constitutional Court annulled that verdict, and the case lapsed in 2016 without a new ruling. In Finland the defendants were acquitted on appeal. An Austrian court convicted one middleman. No court has a standing finding that Janša took bribes.

Opus Dei, the Order of Malta and the Trilateral Commission, a private forum of politicians and business leaders, have a documented presence. So does Azerbaijan's lobbying operation known as 'caviar diplomacy'. No case connects any of them to wrongdoing in Slovenia. Slovenia is in the Moderate band of the Global Organized Crime Index. The index gives it 6.5 of 10 for officials acting for outside interests and 6.2 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.
Slovenia.imp: Slovenian taxpayers paid for an arms contract that a foreign broadcaster said was won with bribes, and courts in three countries reached different conclusions. Because the case lapsed, voters never received a final answer on whether their prime minister took money from a foreign arms maker. They have had to judge him at elections without one.

Spain.d:
In Galicia, clans that had smuggled tobacco began landing cocaine for the Medellín and Cali cartels. Operation Nécora in 1990 led to convictions of several clan leaders. Many defendants were acquitted, and protection by local politicians was alleged but never proven. The landing sites in the Galician rías are still in use.

Around Algeciras, near Gibraltar, cocaine and hashish networks recruit municipal police, customs officers and port workers. In April 2024 a municipal officer and two national police officers were sentenced to more than seven years each for guarding a cocaine load. A 2022 operation arrested five municipal officers at the port, a customs official and others over 6.2 tonnes moved through the strait.

In 2022 the government said Pegasus spyware, which is sold only to governments, had infected the phones of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and Defence Minister Margarita Robles. No state has been officially named, and the High Court reopened the case in 2024.

Foreign minister José Manuel Albares and economy minister Carlos Cuerpo were on the list for the 2024 Bilderberg meeting in Madrid. Jorge Fernández Díaz, interior minister from 2011 to 2016, is reported to be an Opus Dei member.

Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation with lay members. From 1957 its members held Franco's finance and trade ministries and drove the plan that opened Spain's closed economy. After the MATESA credit scandal in 1969, Franco formed a cabinet in which eleven members had Opus Dei ties. Gareth Gore's 2024 book says Banco Popular, led for decades by Opus Dei members, channelled money to Opus Dei causes; Opus Dei calls this false.
Spain.imp: People in Algeciras and the Galician coast live beside police officers and port staff who have been paid by drug networks. Spanish voters do not know which foreign government spied on their prime minister's phone. Shareholders in Banco Popular lost their money when it was sold for €1 in 2017.

Sweden.d: A 2023 research review published by SNS, a Swedish research body, found that criminal networks run companies in the welfare sector, claim social insurance and have people inside government agencies. Wrong welfare payments are estimated at SEK 13–16.3 billion a year. In Södertälje, police saw warning signs in the late 1990s but acted only after a double murder in 2010. Swedish courts have convicted police employees of passing information from police registers to these networks. A Security Service officer was convicted separately of an unauthorised disclosure. Swedbank was fined 4 billion kronor in 2020 over high-risk money flows through its branches in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, and regulators also fined and censured Nordea and SEB's Baltic successors. The Wallenberg family's foundations own about 23% of Investor AB but hold just over half its votes. Through it the family has large or controlling stakes in Ericsson, ABB, Saab, SEB and Electrolux. This control is legal and disclosed. Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson attended the 2025 Bilderberg Meeting in Stockholm, a private conference of politicians and executives, although his name was not on the published list. During the Second World War the government used Wallenberg bankers for its trade talks, and the US seized the bank's American Bosch holding as hidden German property. In 1973 journalists revealed IB, a secret military intelligence bureau that registered left-wing people. The journalists, not IB staff, were convicted of espionage.
Sweden.imp: Residents' taxes fund the welfare payments that criminal-run firms claim, and the losses fall hardest on municipal budgets for care and schools. When police staff pass register data to the networks, people who report crimes or give evidence can be identified by the groups they report. Bank customers in the Baltic states and Sweden saw their banks fined for moving money they had not checked. One family's voting shares decide who sits on the boards of many of the largest employers.

Switzerland.d: In Geneva, Philip Morris documents leaked in 2017 showed the company lobbying delegates to the WHO tobacco treaty and fighting tax and advertising rules. A WHO expert committee had found in 2000 that tobacco firms worked for years to undermine the WHO. The Gates Foundation, a private US charity, was the WHO's second-largest funder in 2020, mostly for programmes it chose. A former UN human rights staff member says the office gave China the names of Chinese activists; the office rejects her claims. In Zurich, FIFA executive committee members took money to vote for Russia and Qatar as World Cup hosts, according to a US indictment. Attorney General Michael Lauber met FIFA's president without keeping records while his office investigated FIFA, and he left office in 2020. Credit Suisse was convicted in 2022 of failing to stop laundering for a Bulgarian cocaine group. Glencore pleaded guilty to bribery in the US and UK, and Trafigura was convicted in Switzerland of failing to prevent bribery in Angola. The UAE paid the Geneva firm Alp Services to discredit about 1,000 people in Europe, partly by feeding their names into bank compliance databases. From 1970 the CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned Crypto AG, a Swiss maker of cipher machines, and read the messages of governments that bought them. A Swiss parliamentary inquiry found that Swiss intelligence knew and benefited. In Basel, central bank governors meet in private at the BIS, whose committee writes the bank capital rules that national regulators adopt. In 1990 parliament found a secret army, P-26, operating outside government control. A judge's report on its work with British intelligence is sealed until 2041.
Switzerland.imp: Swiss residents pay for prosecutors and regulators who keep finding the country's banks and traders handling bribes and drug money. The costs also fall abroad. Governments that bought Crypto AG machines had their messages read for decades. One businessman says a false 'terrorism' listing placed through Alp Services ruined his company. Rules written at the WHO, FIFA and the BIS in Geneva, Zurich and Basel set health spending, sports hosting and bank lending in other countries.

Ukraine.d: Prosecutors charge that managers of Motor Sich, the aircraft-engine maker in Zaporizhzhia, ran hidden channels supplying engines and parts to Russia with Rostec, Russia's state technology corporation. They say its former president, Viacheslav Bohuslaiev, also blocked delivery of a helicopter to Ukraine's military intelligence in 2022. He is on trial for treason. The Russian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate) backs Russia's war. In 2024 parliament banned it in Ukraine and gave linked Ukrainian church bodies nine months to cut ties. Courts have sentenced individual priests. Energoatom is the state nuclear power company. In November 2025 the National Anti-Corruption Bureau said a group led by Timur Mindich, a friend of President Zelensky, took $100 million in kickbacks from its contractors. Zelensky asked the justice and energy ministers to resign, and a former deputy prime minister was charged. In Zakarpattia, customs and border officers are charged with running smuggling channels into the European Union. In 2022 Zelensky agreed that BlackRock, the US asset manager, would help design the plan for public and private investment in rebuilding the country. Ihor Kolomoisky co-owned PrivatBank, Ukraine's largest bank, and was governor of Dnipropetrovsk region in 2014–15. The bank had lent over $1 billion to firms tied to its managers before the state nationalised it in 2016. The US designated him for corruption in 2021. He was arrested in 2023 and charged with fraud, money laundering and embezzling from the bank.
Ukraine.imp: Kickbacks on Energoatom contracts raise the cost of keeping the power on during the war. The PrivatBank bailout of $5.6 billion was paid with public money and IMF support, so taxpayers covered what the bank lost. Smuggling through the western crossings depends on officers being paid to let goods through. Members of parishes tied to Moscow must see their church cut its ties or fall under the ban.

United Kingdom.d: In 2022 MI5 warned MPs that the solicitor Christine Lee worked covertly with the United Front Work Department, the Chinese Communist Party's overseas influence office. She had given donations to Labour MP Barry Gardiner, and her son worked in his office. A businessman excluded in 2023 for covert party work had been Prince Andrew's guest at royal residences. Former MEP Nathan Gill was jailed in 2025 for taking bribes to make pro-Russian statements, on requests said in court to come from Viktor Medvedchuk. Six Bulgarians in Britain were jailed for spying for Russia under a former Wirecard executive. A leaked internal Metropolitan Police report from 2002 said London crime families had corrupt officers in the force; nobody was prosecuted from it. Former Prime Minister David Cameron, paid by Greensill Capital, texted the Chancellor asking for the firm to join a Covid loan scheme. PPE Medpro, referred by a Conservative peer, won £200 million of pandemic contracts and must repay about £122 million. Big Four accounting staff were lent to the Treasury to help write tax law. The Grenfell inquiry found that cladding makers obtained safety certificates on false test results. Met officers and staff must now declare Freemason membership, and the High Court upheld the rule in 2026. In the 19th century the Rothschild bank lent the government money for slave-owner compensation and the Suez Canal shares. The claim that the Rothschilds control governments is an antisemitic theory; historians find a large bank whose lead ended in the 1870s. Historian Carroll Quigley counted followers of Cecil Rhodes and Alfred Milner who held a War Cabinet seat, worked in the prime minister's office and edited The Times.
United Kingdom.imp: Taxpayers paid for protective gowns that went unused. They also lost on the Royal Mail sale, priced so low that new shareholders gained £750 million on the first day. Grenfell residents lived under cladding certified on false tests, and 72 people died. Where crime groups pay police staff, people who report crimes or give evidence can be exposed. When charges such as the Christopher Cash spying case are dropped, the public does not learn what information was passed on.

Vatican City.d: The Holy See runs its own bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), and its own courts. In 2021 the Vatican court convicted a former IOR president, Angelo Caloia, and a lawyer of embezzling from the bank through property sales. It ordered about €38 million forfeited. Cardinal Angelo Becciu, a former senior official of the Secretariat of State, was convicted in 2023 over a €350 million investment in a London building. Prosecutors said brokers and officials cost the Holy See tens of millions in fees. In March 2026 the appeals court annulled the indictment over unpublished papal decrees and undisclosed evidence, and ordered a retrial. A finance commission official was jailed in 2016 for leaking documents to journalists. The Order of Malta is a Catholic order recognised as a sovereign entity, with its own diplomats and UN observer status. In 2017 Pope Francis forced its Grand Master to resign after a dispute over a dismissed official. In 2022 he gave the order a new constitution and appointed its ruling council himself. In the 1980s the IOR was the main shareholder of Banco Ambrosiano, a Milan bank that collapsed. The IOR denied liability but paid its creditors $224 million in 1984. Milan magistrates sought to arrest the IOR's president, Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, in 1987. Italy's top court ruled that the 1929 Lateran Treaty shielded the bank's central bodies, and he was never tried.
Vatican City.imp: Money given to the Holy See was lost through the London building deal and the IOR property sales. Because the Lateran Treaty shields the IOR's central bodies from Italian courts, people harmed by the Ambrosiano collapse could not bring its president to trial. Cases inside the Vatican are judged by courts that answer to the Pope. The Becciu conviction was annulled because papal decrees used in the case had not been published.

North Macedonia.d: The World Economic Forum, which runs the annual Davos meeting, selects people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme. The programme is a five-year network of meetings and courses run with the Forum. Its class of 2025 included Timčo Mucunski, North Macedonia's Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade. Taking part is lawful and is not evidence of wrongdoing. No inquiry has found that the Forum directed his decisions. The Forum gets a sitting foreign minister in a network that also includes business leaders, who can meet him through its events. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a documented presence. The Gülen movement, which Turkey's government pursues abroad, is likely present but undocumented. In neighbouring Kosovo, Turkey obtained the handover of six people it accused of Gülen links. The Global Organized Crime Index places North Macedonia in its Moderate band, with a weak score for officials acting for outside interests.
North Macedonia.imp: Residents have a foreign minister who meets business leaders and other officials through a private forum that publishes no record of those talks. They cannot see what is discussed or whether it shapes trade policy. People linked to the Gülen movement may face pressure from Turkey, as six people did in neighbouring Kosovo.

Antigua and Barbuda.d: R. Allen Stanford ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua. He was convicted in the United States of a $7 billion fraud. A US indictment charges Leroy King, then head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, with taking bribes from Stanford. The commission was the body meant to supervise Stanford's bank. Prosecutors say King ignored the bank's real assets in return for more than $100,000. They also say he helped obstruct an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Antigua extradited King to Houston ten years after the indictment. The charges are an accusation, not a verdict. Stanford gained a supervisor who did not check his books, and his bank could keep taking investors' money. Sun Kian Ip Group, the company of businessman Ng Lap Seng, is recorded as present in Antigua and Barbuda. So is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status that runs medical and aid work. Its presence is lawful. Antigua and Barbuda is in the Low band of the Global Organized Crime Index.
Antigua and Barbuda.imp: Antigua's bank supervisor is accused of taking money from the bank he supervised. Investors who trusted that supervision lost their savings in a $7 billion fraud. If the charges are proven, residents learn that their own regulator was paid to look away while a foreign-run bank took deposits under Antigua's name.

Barbados.d: Nothing is documented yet for Barbados, so this is a best guess. No case shows an outside government, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people in office here. No outside organisation is recorded as present. The United Grand Lodge of England, Britain's main Masonic body, is thought to have lodges on the island, but this has not been confirmed. Membership of a lodge is lawful. Barbados is in the Low band of the Global Organized Crime Index. A lack of documented cases means none has come to light, not that none exists.
Barbados.imp: With no documented case, the cost to residents is unknown. The Low band suggests officials face less outside pressure than in many states. Residents are best protected when they can see who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and who owns the companies registered on the island. Those records let people notice outside money before it shapes decisions.

Belize.d: Belize sells and issues passports through an industry that offers citizenship to foreign buyers. That industry, known as citizenship-by-investment, is recorded as active here. A passport lets its holder travel, open bank accounts and register companies as a Belizean. Prime Minister Dean Barrow removed Elvin Penner, the minister of state for immigration, from his post. Penner was accused of selling and issuing a Belizean passport to Kim Won Hong, a South Korean man who was then in jail in Taiwan. Penner was charged a few months later. The charges were dropped for lack of evidence, and no court found him guilty. The buyer in such a case gains a second nationality and a travel document from a state that did not vet him. The official who sells it gains cash. No other Belizean official is recorded in a documented case. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status that runs medical and aid work, is also recorded as present. Its presence is lawful. Belize is in the Moderate band of the Global Organized Crime Index.
Belize.imp: A passport sold by an official puts a Belizean identity in the hands of a person no one checked. Other countries may then check Belizean travellers more closely, which costs honest residents time and money. Because the case was dropped, residents do not know whether other passports were sold or who bought them.

Colombia.d: In October 2025 the United States designated Colombia's sitting president, Gustavo Petro, under its illicit-drug order, citing a rise in coca growing. Colombia rejected the finding, which is one government's decision and not a verdict. The Cali cartel paid into the 1994 presidential campaign of Ernesto Samper. His campaign treasurer and defence minister were convicted, and Congress cleared Samper himself. From 2006, about 30% of Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the AUC, paramilitaries who also trafficked cocaine. Two former Supreme Court presidents and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were later convicted of taking payments to shelve cases against members of Congress. In Medellín, La Oficina de Envigado, a group that sells debt collection, extortion and murder for hire, keeps its money in farms, coffee, mining and meat firms. US Treasury had named its front companies in eight separate actions by 2018, and new fronts replaced the named ones. A 2020 US designation says an associate of the Gulf Clan, the country's largest cocaine trafficking group, funded mayoral candidates in several towns on the group's orders. In 2023 a prosecutor was charged with holding property in her name for a Gulf Clan front man. Odebrecht, the Brazilian builder, paid into President Santos's 2010 campaign, which he acknowledged in 2017. Chiquita, a US banana company, pleaded guilty in 2007 to paying the AUC. The Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ International, a Pentecostal church founded in Colombia, has its own party, MIRA, with three senators.
Colombia.imp: In Medellín and Córdoba, farms, shops and offices that look ordinary have been fronts holding money for armed groups. Voters in several towns chose between mayoral candidates, some of them paid for by a Gulf Clan associate. People in court have faced judges and prosecutors who took money to shelve cases. Families of people the AUC killed sued Chiquita, which had paid the AUC, and won a civil verdict in Florida in 2024.

Costa Rica.d: In June 2025 a former vice-minister of public security, who later sat as a judge, was arrested on a US extradition request. The US Treasury says he helped move tens of millions of dollars' worth of cocaine from Colombia through Costa Rica to the United States and Europe. It says he used contacts in government to learn about ongoing drug investigations. He is charged, not convicted. Weeks before his arrest, Costa Rica changed its constitution to allow extradition of its own citizens for drug trafficking and terrorism. In the Caribbean lowlands, five police officers stationed at Guapiles and Cariari de Pococi were charged in 2026. Investigators say they warned a trafficking group about raids, checkpoints and investigators' movements. Some of them were recruited for that purpose. Fabricio Alvarado, an evangelical Christian singer, reached the 2018 presidential runoff by opposing an Inter-American Court ruling on same-sex marriage, and lost. He founded the New Republic Party in 2019 and sat in the Legislative Assembly from 2022 to 2026. Opus Dei, the Order of Malta, the Atlas Network and the Catholic group Tradition, Family, Property also have a documented presence. No case involving them is documented here.
Costa Rica.imp: People on the Caribbean side live along a cocaine corridor where some police officers are charged with tipping off traffickers before raids. According to the US Treasury, a senior security official passed information on open drug investigations to traffickers. Costa Ricans charged with drug trafficking abroad can now be extradited, which they could not be before May 2025.

Cuba.d: José Manuel Collera Vento became Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Cuba, the country's main Masonic body, in 2000 after government pressure. In 2011 he said on state television that he worked for state security as 'Agente Gerardo'. He said he was placed in the post so the government could monitor Freemasons. A provincial assembly gave him its highest award the same year. In January 2024, about $19,000 kept for a Masonic retirement home went missing, and the Grand Master was expelled. The Ministry of Justice, which registers associations, then refused to recognise the lodge's newly elected leaders, 14ymedio reported. A former grand official who left Cuba in 2023 said a state-security officer told him agents had watched Cuban lodges for over 40 years. The Order of Malta, a Catholic order, also has a documented presence. Cuba's own intelligence directorate, the DI, is based here. In 1989 a military court convicted General Arnaldo Ochoa and an Interior Ministry colonel of smuggling cocaine through Cuban waters and airspace. The colonel ran the state's hard-currency operations. Both were executed by firing squad in July 1989, and the interior minister was dismissed and jailed.
Cuba.imp: Cuban Freemasons meet in lodges whose leaders may report to state security. Members cannot assume that what they say there stays private. When lodges elect new leaders, the Ministry of Justice can refuse to recognise them. Money members gave for a Masonic retirement home went missing in 2024. The 1989 Ochoa case showed senior officers of the state itself moving cocaine through Cuban territory.

Dominica.d: Dominica sells its citizenship to foreigners who invest money there. OCCRP, a network of investigative reporters, found about 7,700 buyers by 2023, among them Afghanistan's former spy chief and Russians under sanctions. In November 2019 Al Jazeera reported that an Iranian businessman, Alireza Monfared, gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's 2014 election campaign. In return, the report says, Monfared received an ambassador's post and a diplomatic passport. A witness said Skerrit handed the passport over in Kuala Lumpur. Monfared was later jailed in Iran for stealing oil revenue. Skerrit denies any trade. The claim is reported, not proven, and no court has ruled on it. The citizenship and passport-sale industry is the only outside organisation with a documented presence in Dominica. What a buyer gets is a Dominican passport, and in Monfared's case a diplomatic one. Dominica sits in the Low band for organised crime. Its score for officials acting for outside interests is 2.0 of 10.
Dominica.imp: Each passport Dominica sells gives its buyer a new nationality, and buyers have included a former spy chief and sanctioned Russians. If the Al Jazeera report is right, a diplomatic post went to a campaign donor. In that case, people who speak for Dominica abroad can be chosen for money rather than for service to residents. Voters have no way to check what campaign donors receive.

Dominican Republic.d: Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, admitted in the United States in 2016 that it paid 92 million dollars in bribes in the Dominican Republic to win public works. In October 2021 a Dominican court convicted former public works minister Víctor Díaz Rúa and businessman Ángel Rondón, named as the channel for the bribes. Four other defendants were acquitted. An appeal court upheld both convictions in May 2023. Three senior officials of the National Drug Control Agency (DNCD) were arrested while guarding traffickers who were waiting for a shipment bound for Puerto Rico. A navy officer in charge of port security was accused of moving 800 kilograms of drugs to Spain. In 2008 nearly twenty officials, mostly navy, were accused of killing seven Colombian traffickers to take their 1.3 tonnes of drugs. Since 2009 more than 700 DNCD staff have been removed, about 200 of them suspected of trafficking. The national police expelled about 1,400 officers from 2010. Opus Dei, the Order of Malta and Ng Lap Seng's Sun Kian Ip Group also have a documented presence. No case involving them is documented here.
Dominican Republic.imp: Dominicans paid for public works through contracts that carried 92 million dollars in bribes. In ports and coastal areas, some anti-drug agents and navy officers have worked for the traffickers they were meant to stop. The police and the drug agency have removed more than two thousand staff since 2009. Residents cannot be sure the officer in front of them is not paid by traffickers.

Ecuador.d: Drug-trafficking groups paid Ecuadorian judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials to fix cases and protect their members. Prosecutors built the Metastasis case from a trafficker's decrypted phone. In November 2024 the National Court convicted 20 of 21 defendants, including a former head of the Judiciary Council. In Guayas province, a separate case called Purga charged judges and a former legislator over paid-for prison releases; it has not been tried. On the coast, cocaine leaves Guayaquil inside banana shipments, and prosecutors have charged exporters, port staff and customs officials. In Manta, licensed tuna boats meet the gangs' speedboats at sea with fuel, food and medical help. The US Treasury sanctioned the Manta network in August 2026. The US government lists Los Choneros, Los Lobos and the Chone Killers, three Ecuadorian gangs, as terrorist organisations. Foreign companies have paid state officials. Gunvor, a Geneva oil trader, was convicted in Switzerland of corruption in Ecuador and paid US and Swiss penalties. A Vitol trader was convicted in the US of bribing officials at Petroecuador, the state oil company. Former vice-president Jorge Glas is in prison for taking bribes from Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group. In March 2025 President Daniel Noboa announced a deal with Erik Prince, founder of the security firm Blackwater, to support the security forces against gangs. Guillermo Lasso, president until 2023, has been reported as a married lay member of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation.
Ecuador.imp: People who go to court in Ecuador cannot be sure a ruling was not bought. The Metastasis court asked prosecutors to investigate further judges, prosecutors and lawyers named at trial. In Guayaquil and Manta, gangs that pay port and customs staff keep cocaine moving. Ecuador now has three gangs on the US terrorist list. Money paid in bribes at Petroecuador came out of oil sales that fund the state. A foreign private security company now works with the forces that police these gangs.

El Salvador.d: In December 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned El Salvador's prisons director, Osiris Luna, and Carlos Marroquín, head of the government's Social Fabric Reconstruction Unit. It said they negotiated in secret with leaders of the MS-13 and Barrio 18 gangs. According to the Treasury, gang leaders got privileges and money inside the prisons. In return the gangs were to cut the number of killings and support the government at elections. A US indictment of 13 MS-13 leaders, unsealed in February 2023, says the government of El Salvador and prison officials organised the meetings. It says officials released one gang leader whom the United States wanted. It also says the gang backed President Nayib Bukele's party, Nuevas Ideas, in the 2021 election. The newspaper El Faro first reported the talks in 2020. Bukele's government denies any pact, and no court has tried the claims. MS-13 is a transnational gang headquartered in El Salvador. Opus Dei and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, two Catholic organisations, have a documented presence. No case links either of them to wrongdoing here. El Salvador is in the high band of the organised-crime index.
El Salvador.imp: Salvadorans cannot check whether part of the fall in killings came from a deal with the gangs, because no court has heard the evidence. If the US account is right, gang leaders traded fewer public killings and election support for better treatment in prison. One gang leader the United States wanted to try was released instead, according to the indictment. Voters in 2021 did not know of the alleged support for the governing party.

Grenada.d: Grenada sells citizenship to foreign investors and has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen. The citizenship-by-investment industry, which sells passports to people who invest or pay into a state fund, operates here. In November 2019 an Al Jazeera investigation reported that Eric Resteiner, a foreign investor, said he had paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell. Mitchell said he received only 15,000 dollars, to cover travel costs. In the same report, US businessman Leo Ford said a business partner had been offered a diplomatic post in return for kickbacks on state projects. The government denies this. No charge has been brought. The claims rest on the investors' own statements, and Al Jazeera did not report documents that settle who paid what. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a documented presence, which is lawful. Grenada is in the low band of the Global Organized Crime Index. Its courts, police and watchdogs score better there than those of most countries in the region.
Grenada.imp: When a government sells passports and diplomatic titles, foreign buyers may expect favours in return, and residents depend on the prime minister's office to refuse them. No court has tested the Resteiner claims, so Grenadians have only the conflicting accounts of an investor and their prime minister. Contracts on state projects are paid from public funds. If a kickback was asked for, it raised the price of work done for residents.

Guyana.d: In June 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned the gold traders Nazar Mohamed and his son Azruddin, with their firm, Mohamed's Enterprise. The Treasury said they left over 10,000 kg of gold off customs declarations and bribed customs officials. It said they also paid officials for help in court cases and to win state contracts. It sanctioned Mae Thomas, a former permanent secretary of the home affairs ministry, for taking cash and gifts for contracts, gun permits and passports. The Mohameds deny wrongdoing. In June 2025 the Treasury sanctioned six people over cocaine routes through Guyana. They include a serving police officer accused of arranging safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers, and two Colombians who manage hidden airstrips. Cocaine is stored in bunkers on jungle airstrips, often in the Barima-Waini region, and leaves on semi-submersible boats. The US State Department treats Guyana as a close partner but calls corruption there a significant obstacle. None of the 2025 cases has been tried. In the mid-2000s, the trafficker Roger Khan ran an armed group, the Phantom Squad, that operated alongside the state during a period of killings. He was convicted in New York and served 15 years. Guyanese courts never settled the squad's link to the government.
Guyana.imp: Guyanese who deal with customs, the courts or the home affairs ministry for permits and passports may have met officials paid by a large gold business, according to the US. Duty lost on undeclared gold, over 50 million dollars by the Treasury's count, was public money. In Barima-Waini and other interior areas, residents live near airstrips used to move cocaine, and a serving police officer is accused of arranging safe passage. Families of people killed in the mid-2000s have had no court ruling on the Phantom Squad.

Haiti.d: In November 2022 Canada sanctioned Senator Joseph Lambert, former senator Youri Latortue and other politicians for financing armed gangs. The gangs, joined since 2023 in the Viv Ansanm alliance, control much of Port-au-Prince. Those named deny funding gangs. In 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned former president Michel Martelly for sponsoring gangs and drug trafficking. He denies it, and no court has heard the case. A UN panel report released in October 2026 names former legislators Alfredo Junior Antoine and Nenel Cassy as gang backers. It says Antoine armed groups and sponsored a 2025 attack that killed more than 100 people. Both men deny the allegations. The panel says some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information. It says a member of the new Cité Soleil municipal commission is an active gang member. Jimmy Cherizier, a police officer until 2018, now leads the largest gang federation in Port-au-Prince. Guy Philippe, a former police commander, was arrested days after winning a Senate seat and served a US sentence for laundering drug money. He went back into politics after his deportation to Haiti in 2023. Vectus Global, a security company run by Erik Prince, has taken part in raids against gangs, Haitian authorities confirmed in January 2026. Reuters reported that Prince planned to keep staff in Haiti for ten years and help collect taxes.
Haiti.imp: People in Port-au-Prince and the Artibonite live among gangs that some politicians fund and some police officers supply, according to the UN panel. It says former senators' use of gangs drives violence in the Artibonite before elections. Residents of Cité Soleil may have a gang member on their municipal commission. None of the sanctioned politicians has been tried, so the claims stay unresolved. A foreign private company now takes part in police raids, and its reported role in tax collection has not been confirmed.

St. Kitts and Nevis.d: St Kitts and Nevis has sold citizenship to foreign investors since 1984. Under such a programme, a person pays the state or invests locally and receives a passport. The citizenship-by-investment industry is based here. In May 2014 FinCEN, the US Treasury's financial crimes unit, warned that several Iranians under US sanctions had obtained Kittitian passports through the programme. It said the programme 'maintains lax controls'. It also said Iranians kept getting passports after a 2013 suspension. FinCEN withdrew the warning in February 2026, after those passports had expired and the programme was reformed. The warning concerned the citizenship unit's checks on buyers. It did not name any Kittitian official as taking money. No other case of foreign states, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials is documented. St Kitts and Nevis is in the moderate band of the Global Organized Crime Index. Its scores for officials acting for outside interests and for courts, police and watchdogs are both near the middle of the scale.
St. Kitts and Nevis.imp: Citizenship sales pay into the state budget, so the citizenship unit's checks decide what risk comes with that money. When the US named the programme's controls as lax in 2014, the warning concerned a document every Kittitian also carries. It stayed in place until 2026. Residents rely on the government to check who buys citizenship, and on the reform that led the US to withdraw its warning.

St. Lucia.d: Nothing is documented yet, so this is a best guess. No case has been found of foreign states, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Lucia. The country is in the low band of the Global Organized Crime Index. Its score for courts, police and watchdogs is in the middle of the scale. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, has a documented presence, which is lawful. Nearby Grenada and St Kitts and Nevis sell citizenship, and both have had cases tied to those sales.
St. Lucia.imp: With no documented case, residents have no known instance of officials paid or placed from outside. The index measures the risk as low. In neighbouring states, citizenship sales have brought claims of payments to a prime minister and sales of passports to people under sanctions. If St Lucia's own programmes or trade grew in those directions, similar costs could follow here.

St. Vincent and the Grenadines.d: Nothing is documented yet, so this is a best guess. No case has been found of foreign states, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Vincent and the Grenadines. It is in the low band of the Global Organized Crime Index. Its score for officials acting for outside interests is the lowest in this group of countries. Its courts, police and watchdogs score near the middle of the scale. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, has a documented presence, which is lawful.
St. Vincent and the Grenadines.imp: With no documented case, residents have no known instance of officials paid or placed from outside. The index rates the chance of officials acting for outside interests as low. That rating is based on the index's own assessment, not on a court case or investigation here. A case that has not yet come to light would change this estimate.

Suriname.d: Desi Bouterse was convicted in absentia by a Dutch court in 1999 of trafficking almost 500 kilograms of cocaine. With no extradition treaty, he never served the sentence and was later elected president twice. His son Dino headed Suriname's Counter-Terrorism Unit while his father was president. In 2013 the US Drug Enforcement Administration lured Dino to Panama and arrested him. He was convicted in New York of cocaine trafficking and weapons offences. He was also convicted of offering a base in Suriname to people he believed were Hezbollah members; they were DEA informants. He was sentenced to about 16 years. Separately, a Surinamese court gave Desi Bouterse 20 years for the 1982 killing of fifteen political opponents. The sentence was upheld in December 2023. He did not surrender, went into hiding in January 2024, and died in December 2024 without serving either sentence. The US Treasury says semi-submersible boats carry cocaine across the Atlantic from Surinamese and Guyanese ports. South American cocaine networks have a documented presence. The National Endowment for Democracy, a US government-funded foundation, also has a documented presence. Suriname is in the severe band of the organised-crime index.
Suriname.imp: Surinamese elected as president a man already convicted abroad of cocaine trafficking, and his son ran a counter-terrorism unit while dealing cocaine. Families of the fifteen people killed in 1982 waited decades for a final verdict, and the sentence was never carried out. Coastal ports are used to ship cocaine across the Atlantic, according to the US Treasury. The courts, police and watchdogs score low on the index, so residents have weak protection against officials who take traffickers' money.

Argentina.d: Javier Milei, Argentina's president since December 2023, won the Liberty Prize of Fundación Atlas before entering politics. He also spoke at events of Atlas Network partners. The Atlas Network, a US-based group of free-market think tanks, says its Argentine partners helped push his deregulation, tax and labour reforms. That is the network's own claim. His economy minister, Luis Caputo, and central bank president, Santiago Bausili, both worked at JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank. Under Mauricio Macri, the Atlas think tank Fundación Pensar merged into his PRO party. Former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner must stand trial in two cases. One concerns her government's pact with Iran over the AMIA bombing investigation. In the other, the Notebooks case, construction and energy executives say they paid cash to officials for public works contracts. She denies the charges. Around Rosario, the former head of the Santa Fe police was convicted of protecting a drug trafficking network. A federal judge in Oran was convicted of selling rulings to traffickers. During the 1970s, P2, an Italian Masonic lodge led by Licio Gelli, listed senior Argentine officials as members. They included interim president Raúl Lastiri, social welfare minister José López Rega and Admiral Emilio Massera of the junta. Perón's government gave Gelli a diplomatic post. Through Operation Condor, the junta coordinated kidnappings with other dictatorships. An Argentine court convicted 15 officers, including ex-dictator Reynaldo Bignone.
Argentina.imp: Argentines live under economic policy run by former investment bankers and promoted by foreign-linked think tanks. Executives testified to cash deliveries to officials, and prosecutors allege those bribes decided who built public works. Around Rosario, the homicide rate has run several times the national figure since a police chief was convicted of protecting traffickers. In the north, a judge sold rulings that favoured traffickers.

Bahamas.d: In Nassau, Banco Ambrosiano Overseas was a subsidiary of Calvi's Italian bank, Banco Ambrosiano. Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, president of the Vatican Bank, had been one of its directors. After Banco Ambrosiano collapsed, Bahamian banking authorities suspended the Nassau unit. The Nassau and Luxembourg units owed about half of the $1.2 to $1.4 billion lent to Panamanian shell companies. The bank gained an offshore unit through which to book those loans. Today global banks are cutting ties with small Caribbean financial centres faster than anywhere else, citing compliance costs. Remittances and trade payments then move through less transparent channels. The drug money the cuts were meant to stop never depended on those bank links. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, is recorded as present. The United Grand Lodge of England, Britain's main Masonic body, and the defunct bank BCCI are thought to have been active here. Neither is documented. The Bahamas is in the Low band of the Global Organized Crime Index.
Bahamas.imp: When foreign banks drop Bahamian banks as partners, families sending or receiving money from abroad pay more or turn to informal channels. Local businesses find it harder to pay for imports. Honest customers bear the cost of rules aimed at drug money, while that money keeps moving through other routes.

Bolivia.d: Two former heads of Bolivia's anti-narcotics force, the FELCN, have been convicted in US courts of protecting cocaine shipments. Rene Sanabria, who later ran a drug intelligence unit in the Interior Ministry, was caught in a DEA sting and sentenced in Miami. His group had agreed to protect cocaine loads bound for Miami. Maximiliano Davila, who led the FELCN until 2019, was convicted in Manhattan and sentenced to 25 years. Prosecutors showed he moved investigations away from allied traffickers. He also assigned armed FELCN officers to guard cocaine loads. The FATF, an international body that sets rules against money laundering, put Bolivia on its increased-monitoring list. After the 1980 'cocaine coup', Luis Arce Gómez served as interior minister and ran repression. A Rome appeals court gave him a life sentence in the Operation Condor case. Journalist Robert Parry wrote that the Unification Church invested in the coup and that its official Bo Hi Pak met the new ruler, Luis García Meza. That is one writer's account. Opus Dei and Tradition, Family, Property, a Catholic traditionalist movement, are recorded as present. The Brazilian crime group Primeiro Comando da Capital is thought to be active but is not documented.
Bolivia.imp: When the officers paid to stop cocaine shipments guard them instead, residents get no protection from traffickers. Police investigations were moved away from the traffickers that the FELCN chief favoured. Bolivia's listing for weak money-laundering controls can make foreign banks slower and costlier for Bolivian businesses and for families sending money.

Brazil.d: In São Paulo, prosecutors say the PCC, Brazil's largest criminal organisation, owned two city bus companies, Transwolff and UpBus, that ran public transport lines. The city took over both firms in April 2024 and moved to end their contracts. In August 2025 investigators found PCC money held in about forty investment funds, which owned ethanol plants, a port terminal and more than a thousand petrol stations. Prosecutors also say the PCC paid São Paulo civil police officers to shield its members from investigation; those officers are charged, not convicted. In Rio de Janeiro, militias that began as off-duty police protection rackets now tax residents in the areas they control. In February 2026 the Supreme Federal Court convicted a former federal deputy and a state audit court counsellor of ordering the 2018 killing of councillor Marielle Franco. Pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God founded the Republicanos party, which a church bishop, Marcos Pereira, has led since 2018. The Evangelical Parliamentary Front, a cross-party caucus of mostly Pentecostal members, lists 213 of 513 deputies. A 2022 report found that the farm caucus's agenda is drafted by an institute funded by business groups whose members include Bayer, Cargill and JBS. Trafigura, a commodity trader, pleaded guilty in the United States in 2024 to bribing Petrobras staff. In 1962 IBAD, an institute linked to the CIA, paid for opposition candidates' campaigns, and the military took power in 1964. Lula's convictions in the Odebrecht bribery cases were annulled by the Supreme Court in 2021.
Brazil.imp: In São Paulo, bus fares and fuel purchases have paid money into businesses that prosecutors say the PCC owned. Investigators found methanol mixed into petrol sold at stations the group controlled, so drivers paid for fuel that was short and below specification. In west Rio, militias tax the same residents the drug groups tax. Judges and police paid by traffickers have issued rulings and given protection. The evangelical caucus votes as a bloc, and pesticide and meat companies fund the farm caucus's agenda.

Canada.d: Canada's public inquiry into foreign interference reported in January 2025 that China is the most active foreign state interfering in Canadian politics. It said China works through diplomats, proxies and the United Front Work Department, the Communist Party body that courts overseas Chinese communities. The same inquiry cited intelligence that proxy agents of India's government may have given illicit money to Canadian politicians. A 2024 parliamentary committee report said some unnamed MPs and senators knowingly took part in foreign interference. The inquiry later found no evidence of traitors in Parliament. In Surrey, British Columbia, Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar was shot dead in 2023. Canada expelled six Indian diplomats in 2024, saying Indian agents passed information on targets to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. India denies this. In 2023 Canada expelled a Chinese diplomat in Toronto over a plan to target MP Michael Chong's relatives in Hong Kong. In Montreal, construction firms paid a share of city contracts to the Rizzuto Mafia, a public inquiry reported in 2015. Border officers at the Windsor and Pacific Highway crossings have been convicted of waving vehicles through. Cameron Ortis, a civilian RCMP intelligence director, was convicted in 2023 of offering secret material to targets. Prime Minister Mark Carney worked at Goldman Sachs for 13 years before joining the Bank of Canada. Protestant and Catholic brotherhoods once filled public offices with their members. Every Toronto mayor in the first half of the 20th century belonged to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity. A secret francophone order, the Ordre de Jacques-Cartier, placed members in federal posts until it dissolved in 1965.
Canada.imp: Sikh Canadians and Chinese Canadians have been watched and targeted in Canada by people that Canadian officials link to the governments of India and China. Voters in some ridings may have chosen candidates whose nominations or campaigns foreign proxies helped. In Montreal, public works contracts carried a cut for the Mafia and for political parties. In British Columbia, casinos accepted bags of cash for years while regulators and the provincial government knew and did not act.

Chile.d: Chile's president since March 2026, José Antonio Kast, is a member of the Schoenstatt Movement, a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany. His under-secretary of justice, Luis Silva, is a numerary member of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation. Membership of these lawful groups is not wrongdoing, and no direction of policy by either group is documented. Under President Piñera, education minister Joaquín Lavín was also an Opus Dei member. Cristián Larroulet moved from Libertad y Desarrollo, a Santiago think tank partnered with the US-based Atlas Network, to a cabinet post in 2010. SQM, a lithium and fertiliser miner whose main shareholder is Pinochet's former son-in-law, paid politicians across the spectrum through fake invoices. It settled US bribery charges in 2017, and in 2024 it agreed a long-term lithium partnership with the state copper company Codelco. In Santiago and the northern border region, prosecutors have charged Carabineros police officers with reselling seized drugs and protecting dealers. Chile has become a transit route for drugs as well as a market. Economists trained under a US-funded University of Chicago programme ran Pinochet's finance and economy ministries and the central bank from 1975. One of them, Miguel Kast, was the president's brother. Pinochet's intelligence service, DINA, called the founding meeting of Operation Condor, a cooperation between South American military intelligence services, in Santiago in 1975. DINA held prisoners at Colonia Dignidad, a German sect compound near Parral, where some residents helped torture them.
Chile.imp: Chile's economy was rebuilt from 1975 on a plan written by economists trained under a US-funded programme. Voters across many parties were represented by politicians whose campaigns SQM paid through fake invoices. The same company now holds a long-term lithium deal with the state. In Santiago and the north, some officers charged with reselling seized drugs belong to the police force residents call for help. Families of people held at Colonia Dignidad waited from the 1991 truth commission until 2013 for the Supreme Court to order prosecutions.

Guatemala.d: The head of Guatemala's anti-narcotics police and his deputy were arrested in the United States in 2005 and pleaded guilty to cocaine trafficking. José Armando Ubico, a member of Congress, admitted in a Texas court in 2024 that he passed cash and information for a trafficker. The mayor of Santa Lucía in Escuintla admitted using municipal letterhead to help a cocaine shipment avoid inspection. Near the Mexican border, the US Treasury sanctioned a serving mayor and the Los Pochos group, which supplies the Sinaloa Cartel, along with nine Guatemalan companies. Freddy Salazar, a deputy in the Central American Parliament, faces a US cocaine charge and has not been tried. In Guatemala City, two import firms were sanctioned in 2026 for moving fentanyl chemicals from India for the Sinaloa Cartel. Former vice-president Roxana Baldetti faces a US cocaine charge that has not been tried; she denies it. She is held in Guatemala on two corruption convictions. CICIG, a UN-backed commission, helped prosecutors expose a customs-bribery ring that forced President Otto Pérez Molina to resign in 2015. President Jimmy Morales ended CICIG in 2019 while it was investigating his campaign funds. By 2023 more than thirty judges and prosecutors who worked those cases had left the country under threat of arrest. Earlier, Mario Sandoval Alarcón, a leader of the World Anti-Communist League, was vice-president in the 1970s. Historians link his party to the Mano Blanca death squad. Héctor Trujillo, a judge and football official, pleaded guilty in the US FIFA bribery case.
Guatemala.imp: Guatemalans who report a crime may be dealing with police, mayors or legislators paid by traffickers. Since CICIG closed and its partner prosecutors left, cases against powerful officials have no court at home, and most now go to US courts. In border towns, groups such as Los Pochos take part in local politics. Chemicals brokered through Guatemala City become fentanyl. In the La Línea customs case, bribes meant import duties that should have reached the treasury went to officials instead.

Honduras.d: Juan Orlando Hernández, president from 2014 to 2022, was convicted in New York of conspiring to import cocaine and sentenced to 45 years. He received a US presidential pardon in December 2025 and was released. Honduras then asked Interpol to arrest him on a domestic warrant. His brother Tony, a former congressman, was sentenced to life in New York. Trial evidence said cocaine money funded the National Party's campaigns. Juan Carlos Bonilla, national police chief in 2012–2013, pleaded guilty to taking payments to protect cocaine loads. Fabio Lobo, son of President Porfirio Lobo, is serving 24 years for arranging police escorts for shipments. Porfirio Lobo was named by witnesses in those trials and placed on a US list of corrupt actors, but has never been charged. Banco Continental, owned by the family of a former vice-president, was sanctioned by the US as a laundering bank for the Cachiros trafficking group. Honduran regulators closed it within days. Yani Rosenthal, a congressman from that family, pleaded guilty in New York and served three years. The US also sanctioned the Los Valles family group, which moved cocaine north through Honduras. Rafael Callejas, president from 1990 to 1994 and later head of the football federation, pleaded guilty in the US FIFA case to taking bribes. In 1984 the armed forces chief, General Gustavo Álvarez Martínez, led a group called APROH. It received money from a front for the Unification Church, a religious movement. Fellow officers removed him that year.
Honduras.imp: Hondurans have had a president, a police chief and members of Congress who took money to let cocaine pass, according to US courts. Trial evidence said elections were partly paid for with drug money. When Banco Continental was closed, depositors were paid out over the following year. The main cases were tried abroad, and the former president was pardoned and released. Hondurans have not seen these officials tried at home.

Jamaica.d: The Jamaican government spent nine months resisting a US request to extradite Christopher Coke, leader of the Shower Posse gang, whose base was Tivoli Gardens in West Kingston. It hired a Washington law firm to lobby against the request. When the security forces went into Tivoli Gardens, at least 69 people were killed. Coke pleaded guilty in New York in 2011. The West Kingston Commission of Enquiry, reporting in 2016, found the operation unjustified in its conduct. The prime minister had already resigned over the affair. Earlier, under Prime Minister Edward Seaga, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) handled Jamaica's US commodity financing and most government foreign-currency accounts. A BCCI officer told the US Senate that the bank handled every penny of foreign currency coming into or out of Jamaica. The Senate's 1992 report lists BCCI loans to the Bank of Jamaica and to Petrojam, the state oil company. The United Grand Lodge of England, the main Freemason body, and the Rhodes Trust, which funds overseas scholarships, are likely present, but no case is documented. Jamaica is in the high band of the organised-crime index.
Jamaica.imp: In West Kingston, residents lived under a gang leader whom their government shielded from extradition for nine months. The operation that ended it killed at least 69 people, and the commission found its conduct unjustified. Residents waited until 2016 for that finding. When one foreign bank handled most of the state's foreign currency and lent to the central bank and Petrojam, the country's import and fuel payments depended on that bank.

Mexico.d: In April 2026 a New York court charged Rubén Rocha Moya, then governor of Sinaloa, with protecting the Chapitos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. Nine other officials were charged with him, including a senator and the mayor of Culiacán. Prosecutors say cartel members stole ballot boxes to help him win in 2021. He denies it, resigned, and is not in custody. Genaro García Luna, federal security minister until 2012, was convicted in New York of taking Sinaloa Cartel payments. In Nayarit, the state attorney general pleaded guilty to working for a cartel, and the US sanctioned the governor. In Tabasco, the former state security chief is accused of running a CJNG-linked gang from his office. In Iguala, municipal police working for Guerreros Unidos took 43 students who then disappeared. In Jalisco, Nayarit, Michoacán and Zacatecas, the US sanctioned tequila distilleries, agave farms and gas stations as fronts for the CJNG cartel. A resort near Puerto Vallarta passed its timeshare buyers' details to cartel call centres that defrauded them. In Michoacán, gangs charge avocado and lime growers a fee per hectare. Naval officers and customs officials were arrested over fuel imported under false labels through navy-run ports. Emilio Lozoya, former head of the state oil company Pemex, is accused of taking bribes from Odebrecht; he denies it. A Vitol oil trader was convicted in the US of bribing Pemex officials. Writers have claimed that El Yunque, a secret Catholic group, had members among PAN party leaders and in Vicente Fox's cabinet. The PAN denies it. In the 1940s the Rockefeller Foundation started a farm programme with the government that became the Green Revolution.
Mexico.imp: In Sinaloa, Nayarit, Tabasco and Guerrero, residents have had governors, prosecutors, security chiefs or local police who worked for cartels, according to US and Mexican courts. Municipal police forces in Michoacán, Guerrero and Tamaulipas have been disbanded for working for cartels. Farmers in Michoacán pay gangs for each hectare. Many cases against Mexican officials are tried only in the United States. The US dropped its case against a former defence minister after Mexico objected, and Mexico's own inquiry closed without charges.

Nicaragua.d: Russia's Interior Ministry opened a police training centre in Managua in 2017. The president's son, Laureano Ortega Murillo, attended the opening. The centre trains Nicaraguan police and officers from other Central American and Caribbean countries. In May 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned it. The Treasury said it trains officials of the Ortega-Murillo government under the Russian government's 'playbook of oppression' and helps repress civil society. In the 1980s, the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), a US government-funded foundation, gave about $2 million to Nicaragua's civic opposition. About half went to La Prensa, the newspaper run by Violeta Chamorro. In 1989 the US House voted for President Bush's plan to spend a further $9 million on the opposition before the 1990 election. Chamorro's National Opposition Union won that election. NED says its grants are public and nonpartisan. Before that, Banco Ambrosiano, the bank of the Italian banker Roberto Calvi, ran a bank in Managua. It gave money to both the Somoza government and the Sandinista opposition. In 1985 President Daniel Ortega cancelled its licence by decree. Opus Dei and the Unification Church also have a documented presence. Nicaragua is in the severe band of the organised-crime index, with the lowest score for courts, police and watchdogs in this group.
Nicaragua.imp: Nicaraguans deal with police trained at a Russian government centre that the US says teaches the repression of civil society. People who join protests, unions or independent groups face that police force. The president's family attended its opening. Officers from neighbouring countries also train there. In the 1980s, US public money paid for much of the opposition press and campaign before the 1990 vote, so voters then were choosing between sides funded in part from abroad.

Panama.d: Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group, says it paid $59 million to Panamanian officials during Ricardo Martinelli's 2009–2014 government. The main money-laundering trial opened in January 2026 with more than 20 defendants. Martinelli, who has asylum in Colombia, joined by video and pleaded innocent. Former president Juan Carlos Varela and two of Martinelli's sons will be tried separately by the Supreme Court. Panamanian law firms form companies for clients abroad. Mossack Fonseca, the firm at the centre of the Panama Papers, was acquitted with its founders in 2024. The judge found the evidence insufficient and improperly gathered. Alcogal, which became the region's largest company formation agent, appeared throughout the Pandora Papers. It had formed thousands of companies without checking who really owned them. It says it followed the law in force, and it has not been charged. In the Colón Free Zone, goods pass without entering Panamanian customs. The US has sanctioned traders there for laundering drug money. In 2016 Panama seized Balboa Bank & Trust after the US sanctioned it with the Grupo Wisa trading group. General Manuel Noriega, head of state from 1983 to 1989, was convicted in Miami of drug trafficking after the US invasion. He kept about $25 million at the bank BCCI in an account in the name of the Defense Forces. He also had BCCI pay off the mortgage of Nicolás Ardito Barletta, who became president in 1984.
Panama.imp: Panamanians paid for public works on which Odebrecht says it paid bribes. The former president accused in that case is taking part in his trial from asylum abroad. The company-formation and free-zone trades bring work, and they also bring clients who hide drug money. When Balboa Bank was seized in 2016, it was wound down. Under Noriega, a president's mortgage was paid off by a bank acting on the army chief's orders.

Paraguay.d: In January 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned former president Horacio Cartes and the sitting vice-president, Hugo Velázquez, for corruption. It said both had ties to members of Hezbollah, a Lebanese armed movement and party. It said their representatives collected bribes at private Hezbollah events in Paraguay. The US lifted the sanctions on Cartes and several of his companies in 2025. In Ciudad del Este, in the Tri-Border Area, the US sanctioned the Barakat trading network, and Argentina froze its assets in 2018. Free-zone paperwork there lets goods, invoices and value move without matching cargo. A 2022 investigation called A Ultranza Py charged police officers, prosecutors, court officials and a member of the Chamber of Deputies over a cocaine network using the Hidrovía river route. Hundreds of properties were seized. The central figure fled before arrest, and the cases continue. Under the dictator Alfredo Stroessner, Paraguay's central bank kept money at BCCI. BCCI's ties there came through the Saudi businessman Ghaith Pharaon, a friend of Stroessner. In 1992 a lawyer and a judge found the files of Stroessner's secret police in a police station in Lambaré, outside Asunción. The files proved that Operation Condor, a joint programme of South American dictatorships to track and kill opponents, existed. In 2005 the Senate voted to expropriate land around Puerto Casado that the Unification Church had bought.
Paraguay.imp: Paraguayans have seen a former president and a sitting vice-president sanctioned by the US for corruption. The sanctions on Cartes were then lifted without any court ruling either way. Prosecutors and court officials charged in the A Ultranza Py case worked in the justice system residents rely on, and one of the case's own prosecutors was removed. The residents of Puerto Casado lived in a town owned by a foreign church until the Senate vote.

Peru.d: Former president Alejandro Toledo was sentenced in 2024 to 20 years for taking about $35 million from Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group, in return for the Interoceanic Highway contract. Former president Ollanta Humala and his wife Nadine Heredia were each sentenced to 15 years for laundering money linked to Odebrecht. Both deny it, and Heredia has asylum in Brazil. In Callao, wiretaps from 2018 recorded a supreme court judge, the Callao court president and members of the judicial appointments council trading sentence cuts and promotions. The first trial conviction came in November 2025. In Junín, prosecutors say a network in the regional transport office sold driving licences and passed the fees to the Perú Libre party. Its leader, Vladimir Cerrón, is a fugitive in another case. ENACO, the state coca company, pays farmers less than traffickers do, so most leaf leaves the legal channel, researchers found. Rafael López Aliaga, an Opus Dei member, was mayor of Lima and is now a senator. In July 2025 a TV programme reported that Prime Minister Eduardo Arana holds a high Freemason rank and that his ministry hired a lodge member. Arana said the hire met the job's requirements. Under President Alberto Fujimori, intelligence chief Vladimiro Montesinos controlled much of the military, courts and press. He was later convicted of drug trafficking and of sending rifles to Colombian guerrillas. In 1987 Peru's central bank kept reserves at BCCI, and a US indictment alleged bribes for the deposits.
Peru.imp: Peruvians have seen two former presidents convicted over money from a foreign builder, and the Interoceanic Highway contract was awarded in return for a bribe. In Callao, people facing court could not be sure a sentence reduction had not been traded. In Junín, drivers may have bought licences through a network rather than earning them. Coca farmers in the main legal valley sell most of their leaf to traffickers, who pay more than the state company.

Trinidad and Tobago.d: Nothing is documented yet of outside groups placing people inside Trinidad and Tobago's own government offices, so this is a best guess. The one related case concerns Jack Warner. He was a FIFA vice-president and also sat in the cabinet, as works minister and then national security minister, until 2013. The US charged him in 2015 with fraud, racketeering and money laundering, including a $10 million payment tied to South Africa's World Cup bid. FIFA banned him for life. Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition in 2025, and he has not been tried. The country is in the moderate band of the organised-crime index.
Trinidad and Tobago.imp: Trinidadians had a national security minister who was later charged abroad with taking bribes as a football official. Because the High Court blocked his extradition, the charges have not been tested in any court. The index puts the risk of officials acting for outside interests in the middle of the scale. Residents have no other documented case to judge it by.

United States.d: In Ohio, the power company FirstEnergy paid about $60 million to a group around the Republican House Speaker, Larry Householder, for a law rescuing its nuclear plants; he is in prison. In Illinois, Commonwealth Edison gave jobs and contracts to associates of the Democratic Speaker, Michael Madigan, since convicted of bribery. New Jersey's Democratic senator Bob Menendez took gold bars and cash and passed sensitive information to help Egypt's government; he is serving 11 years. In Arcadia, California, Mayor Eileen Wang pleaded guilty to acting as an agent of China; her campaign treasurer is in prison. Linda Sun, a former aide to New York's governor, was charged as a Chinese agent; her first trial ended without a verdict. Hackers attributed to China's Ministry of State Security got into the networks of AT&T, Verizon and other carriers. North Korea placed its programmers in more than 300 US firms through a laptop farm in Arizona. Border officers at ports of entry keep being convicted for letting cartel loads through. People who wrote or advised on the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025, a conservative governing plan, run the budget office, the CIA and other agencies under Trump. Nearly 70 staff of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic-aligned think tank, joined the Biden administration. Trump wrote that he used the Federalist Society, a network of conservative lawyers, as his source for choosing judges. The Justice Department dropped its fraud case against Boeing for deceiving aviation regulators about the 737 MAX. From the 1950s until 1967 the CIA secretly paid for the National Student Association and passed money through foundations. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan helped elect governors in Indiana, Colorado and Oregon.
United States.imp: People in Ohio pay power bills set by a law passed in return for company money. Officials paid by a company or a foreign government vote and write rules for the payer. A foreign spy service has had access to Americans' call records through hacked telecom systems. Firms that hired North Korean workers paid wages that went to that state's weapons programmes. When prosecutors drop cases against companies such as Boeing, airline passengers carry the risk.

Uruguay.d: Philip Morris International, the tobacco company based in Lausanne, sued Uruguay in 2010 at the World Bank's investment tribunal. It said Uruguay's large health warnings on cigarette packs harmed its trademarks. The tribunal ruled for Uruguay in 2016 and ordered the company to pay Uruguay's costs. The case is cited as the leading example of a tobacco company using an investment treaty against a health law. No current case shows outside groups with people inside Uruguay's government. Uruguay is in the Low band for organised crime. The other documented cases date from military rule. In 1981 the Unification Church, the Korean religious movement led by Sun Myung Moon, bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of Uruguay's oldest banks. It also founded a daily paper that backed the military government. A parliamentary commission later found the bank had lent about US$100 million to Moon-linked companies before it closed in 2002. That same year Uruguayan police seized files at the Montevideo villa of Licio Gelli, head of the Italian P2 Masonic lodge, who had fled there. Under Operation Condor, the joint repression plan of South American military governments, prisoners were moved from Uruguay to Argentina. The last military president, Gregorio Álvarez, was convicted of 37 homicides in 2009. A Rome court gave former foreign minister Juan Carlos Blanco a life sentence in 2019, subject to appeal.
Uruguay.imp: Uruguay kept its health warnings and did not pay the tobacco company, but it had to defend a case lasting six years. Families of people disappeared under military rule have seen a former president and a former foreign minister sentenced. Banco de Crédito, one of the oldest banks in the country, failed in 2002 after lending heavily to companies linked to the church that owned almost half of it.

Venezuela.d: On 3 January 2026 US forces seized President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores in Caracas and flew them to New York to face drug charges. Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez became interim president. In October 2025 President Trump had confirmed that he had authorised CIA covert action inside Venezuela. Congress did not authorise the operation. US prosecutors charged Maduro and more than a dozen officials in 2020, saying senior officers ran cocaine shipments as a group called the Cartel de los Soles. Analysts dispute that it is an organised cartel, and the charges have not been tried. Diosdado Cabello, interior minister since 2024, is named in the same indictment. Néstor Reverol was charged in New York in 2015 with warning traffickers of raids while he headed the anti-drug office, and was then made interior minister. Former military intelligence chief Hugo Carvajal pleaded guilty in New York in 2025. Cuba signed agreements in 2008 to restructure Venezuela's military intelligence, which then turned to watching Venezuela's own officers. Reuters reported in 2026 that Cuban advisers were leaving those posts. Odebrecht, the Brazilian builder, told Brazilian prosecutors it gave $35 million to Maduro's 2013 campaign in return for priority on its projects. No Venezuelan court has examined that claim. Since Maduro's capture the United States markets Venezuelan oil into US-controlled accounts and licenses selected companies. The government hired Rothschild & Co in 2024 to list who is owed its defaulted foreign debt. In 2002 the director of Cedice, a Caracas think tank funded through the US National Endowment for Democracy, signed the decree of the short-lived coup government.
Venezuela.imp: Venezuelans had their head of state removed by a foreign military before any trial on the charges against him. Oil sales now pay into accounts controlled by the United States, which decides what the government receives. The police, the anti-drug office and military intelligence have been led by men US prosecutors charge with drug trafficking. Soldiers who disagreed with the government were watched by an intelligence service restructured under Cuban supervision.

Kosovo.d:
On 29 March 2018 Kosovo police and intelligence officers seized five teachers and a doctor and flew them to Turkey on a private plane. Turkey's government had accused them of links to the movement of preacher Fethullah Gülen, which it calls a terrorist group. Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj said he had not been told and sacked the interior minister and the intelligence chief. In 2023 a court in Pristina sentenced former intelligence chief Driton Gashi to four years and eight months for abuse of office. Turkey got six people it wanted, by using Kosovo's own security services.

In 2010 Swiss senator Dick Marty reported to the Council of Europe that a 'Drenica Group' of former Kosovo Liberation Army commanders controlled criminal trades including heroin. He said the group was led by then Prime Minister Hashim Thaçi. He also found 'credible, convergent indications' of organ trafficking from captives after the 1999 war. Thaçi denied it. An EU task force later reported compelling indications of war crimes, and Thaçi has been on trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers since 2023. The organised-crime claims have not been tested in court.

The Global Organized Crime Index does not score Kosovo, so North Macedonia's figures are used as a stand-in.
Kosovo.imp: People living in Kosovo learned that their intelligence service could hand them to another government without a court hearing. Five teachers and a doctor were removed from the country without a hearing. If the Marty report is right, a former prime minister's circle profited from heroin, and residents have still not had a court ruling on that claim.
